abstracts.value: This dissertation presents a search for low-energy neutrinos in temporal coincidence with gravitational wave events reported by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration during the fourth observing run (O4), using 499.0 days of data collected during the liquid scintillator phase of the SNO+ experiment. The search uses inverse beta decay (IBD), which is primarily sensitive to electron antineutrinos, and neutrino-proton elastic scattering, a complementary neutral current channel providing sensitivity to all neutrino flavors. Candidate events were identified using optimized reconstruction and event-selection criteria developed with Monte Carlo simulations and validated with background-only data. The IBD background rate was measured directly from data, naturally incorporating reactor antineutrinos, geoneutrinos, radioactive backgrounds, cosmogenic backgrounds, and accidental coincidences present during detector operation. A model-independent framework was developed using flat spectrum neutrino Monte Carlo samples, allowing the detector response to be evaluated as a function of neutrino energy and applied to different theoretical emission models. As part of this work, improvements were made to the SNO+ Monte Carlo simulation, including modifications to the IBD generator to produce a true flat neutrino spectrum and corrections to the implementation of the neutrino-proton elastic scattering cross section. Detector characterization studies, including measurements of the deployed scintillator light yield and investigations of detector timing and electronics performance, were also performed to validate the detector response used throughout the analysis. The final gravitational wave-coincident dataset contained 143 candidates overlapping stable SNO+ data-taking periods. After excluding candidates classified as terrestrial or unknown by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration, the final astrophysical sample used for compact binary merger fluence limits contained 126 gravitational wave candidates. No statistically significant neutrino excess was observed in either the IBD or neutrino-proton elastic scattering channels. The IBD search observed no coincident candidates in the final astrophysical gravitational wave sample, consistent with an expected background of 1.25 ± 0.09 events. The corresponding Feldman-Cousins 90% confidence level upper limit is N90stack = 1.47 signal events. Stacked average (per gravitational wave) upper limits on the electron antineutrino fluence were derived for both monoenergetic neutrino emission and model-dependent spectra, including thermal neutrino and core-collapse supernova-inspired models used as detector sensitivity benchmarks. The neutrino-proton elastic scattering search represents the first application of this all-flavor channel to a gravitational wave-coincident neutrino search. Using an optimized ±50 s coincidence window, 108424 candidate events were observed, consistent with the expected background of 108345 ± 786 events estimated from local sidebands. The observed 0.24σ fluctuation is consistent with the background-only hypothesis. For the final astrophysical gravitational wave sample, the Feldman-Cousins method gives a 90% confidence level upper limit of N90stack = 1479.6 signal events. These results are used to derive the first all-flavor neutrino-proton elastic scattering fluence limits associated with compact binary merger candidates. The resulting SNO+ IBD fluence limits improve upon previous liquid scintillator gravitational wave-neutrino searches by approximately an order of magnitude in the few-MeV energy region, primarily due to the larger fiducial target mass, increased gravitational wave sample size, and low background rate achieved in SNO+. The neutrino-proton elastic scattering results establish the first all-flavor MeV neutrino search through this interaction channel in coincidence with gravitational wave events. Together, these analyses extend previous multi-messenger searches performed by Borexino, KamLAND, and Super-Kamiokande and demonstrate the capability of SNO+ to search for weak neutrino signals associated with astrophysical transients.

titles.title: The Search for Mev-scale Neutrinos in Temporal Coincidence With o4 Gravitational Wave Events Using the Sno+ Experiment

abstracts.value: Realistic simulation of quantum key distribution (QKD) networks requires a combination of precise models of quantum channels and network functions. Unfortunately, existing QKD network simulators lack either rigorous quantum physics modeling or network key-management and routing protocols, which limit their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose a QKD network simulator with hyperparameter tuning (QKDSim-HT), a NetSquid-based simulator specialized for polarization-based discrete-variable QKD networks. Specifically, QKDSim-HT models properties in quantum physics (photon loss, polarization-dependent depolarization, detector inefficiencies, dark counts, and dead times) as well as advanced functionalities in networking algorithms (multi-hop key relay and adaptive routing). Extensive simulations over diverse topologies reveal that the networking performance varied with respect to the fundamental properties of quantum physics, such as depolarization, fiber length, and channel attenuation. As a representative use case of QKDSim-HT, simulation results from QKDSim-HT over simple examples clearly manifest that a design of QKD networks highly affects performance of the networks. Accordingly, QKDSim-HT can serve as a practical platform for performance evaluation and optimization of quantum secured network.

titles.title: Quantum Key Distribution Network Simulator With Hyperparameter Tuning for Realistic Performance Analysis

abstracts.value: We present a unified theoretical framework for analyzing both electrostatic two-stream and electromagnetic Weibel instabilities in counterstreaming electron-positron pair plasmas. Through systematic derivation of dispersion relations in non-relativistic and relativistic regimes, we demonstrate how the symmetric mass ratio fundamentally alters instability characteristics compared to electron-ion systems. The two-stream instability, driven by longitudinal electrostatic perturbations parallel to beam motion, exhibits enhanced growth rates in pair plasmas due to equal contributions from both species, with relativistic suppression scaling as γ0−3 for both electrons and positrons. The Weibel instability, arising from transverse electromagnetic modes perpendicular to streaming directions, lacks the heavy-ion stabilization present in electron-ion plasmas, producing broader unstable spectral ranges and modified saturation levels. We derive explicit conditions determining the relative dominance of each mechanism across parameter space defined by drift velocity, wavenumber orientation, and relativistic Lorentz factor. Our analysis shows that longitudinal two-stream modes dominate at small perpendicular wavenumbers and moderate drift velocities, while transverse Weibel modes become prevalent at high perpendicular wavenumbers and large velocity spreads or temperature anisotropies. These findings have direct implications for understanding magnetic field generation, particle acceleration, and energy dissipation in astrophysical pair plasmas including pulsar wind nebulae, gamma-ray burst internal shocks, and active galactic nuclei jets where counterstreaming pair populations naturally arise.

titles.title: Suppression of two-stream and Weibel instabilities in ultra-relativistic electron–positron plasma

abstracts.value: Realistic quantum devices are open systems, and their behaviour depends not only on the subsystem of interest but also on how the environment is modelled and how the relevant observables are extracted. This thesis studies that problem in three settings. First, we study cavity-assisted qubit readout beyond the dispersive regime. We show that once coherent excitation exchange and dissipation become relevant, a microscopic treatment is needed to describe the readout quantitatively, and the optimal readout is set by a trade-off between signal accumulation and the distinguishability of the readout states. Second, we compare fermionic and spin baths in non-interacting transport models and show that spin baths reproduce fermionic reduced dynamics only in the large-bath weak-coupling limit, while clear deviations appear for smaller baths and near half-filling. Third, we study charge transport in molecular junctions using Automated Compression of Environments (ACE). There, the main difficulty is not the time evolution itself, but the extraction of the transport current, since this observable depends on system-environment correlations and is therefore not contained in the reduced system density matrix alone. We show that a probe-mode construction provides a viable route to reformulate the current as a system observable. This thesis advances our understanding of what is required for accurate modelling of open quantum dynamics across a range of solid-state settings, from cavity-assisted qubit readout to charge transport in molecular junctions.

titles.title: Developing and validating models of open quantum systems in solid-state nanostructures

abstracts.value: Using superconducting rectifiers to energize high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets is a promising approach to accelerate the uptake of HTS magnet technology. In this work, we start to address two limitations of the HTS superconducting rectifier concepts published to date; their low magnet charging voltages, and the variable properties of their HTS-based switches. Our approach is to test a centre-tapped full-wave transformer–rectifier utilizing HTS secondary windings and switch-arrays of Si <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small>s mounted on a printed-circuit board (PCB). This approach has the advantage of greatly facilitating reproducible and reliable manufacture. The rectifier demonstrated magnet charging voltages exceeding a cycle-averaged 80 mV at 100 A and with typically more than 30% of the power supplied to the primary coils delivered to the magnet. We found it to be resilient to our preliminary thermal-cycling testing, with no degradation in performance observed over eight liquid-nitrogen to ambient (77–295 K) thermal cycles. We compare the impact of voltage- and current-controlled modes for the rectifier’s power supply. Our conclusion is that superconducting rectifiers using <sc xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">mosfet</small> switch arrays placed on PCBs is a very promising approach for low-current HTS magnet power supplies.

titles.title: Using Printed Circuit Boards and MOSFET Switch Arrays Toward the Reliable Manufacture of Superconducting Rectifiers

abstracts.value: Compact high turns ratio superconducting transformers are used to transfer power between low-current copper/ semiconductor-based circuits and high-current superconductor-based circuits. This type of transformer is a key component in devices, such as superconducting transformer rectifiers and superconducting current source inverters. Typically the copper winding and the superconducting winding are arranged with a turn ratio above 100:1, respectively, and are situated entirely within a cryogenic environment. The ohmic losses associated with the high count copper winding is problematic for most cryogenic applications and demands attention even when low currents on the order of 1–10 A are used. To address this problem, a transformer has been made using rare-earth barium copper oxide (REBCO) high-temperature superconductor (HTS) coated conductor for both the primary and secondary windings. The coupling coefficient and power consumption of this transformer were measured and compared to an equivalent transformer consisting of a copper primary winding and HTS secondary winding. The HTS primary was found to provide a significant reduction in transformer power consumption and a slight improvement to transformer coupling at frequencies below <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. An increased transformer core loss and winding AC loss began to negate these efficiency improvements above <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim$</tex-math></inline-formula>8 Hz. In addition, cowinding the primary and secondary windings provided a higher coupling coefficient and lower power consumption for all winding combinations and frequencies tested. Finally, a short discussion on the implications of these findings respect to superconducting transformer rectifiers contextualizes the findings.

titles.title: Compact High Turns Ratio Superconducting Transformer: Comparison Between Cu and REBCO Winding Materials

abstracts.value: The development of large-scale superconducting quantum computers critically depends on the accurate readout of qubit states. To enable this, cryogenic parametric amplifiers have been proposed and developed, and have since found widespread use in small-signal detection applications. Among various amplifier architectures, Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) are widely adopted due to their broad bandwidth, high saturation power, and compatibility with superconducting qubits. In this work, we present a design workflow of JTWPAs based on a cosimulation approach combining electromagnetic (EM) and circuit-level simulation. We apply this method to a uniform JTWPA, comparing our simulation results with experimental data. To mitigate the challenge of constructing lumped-element circuit models usually used in the conventional simulation method, we directly perform full EM analysis of the device to accurately determine its linear response. The extracted S-parameters are then fed into a nonlinear harmonic balance simulator with Josephson junctions modeled as circuit elements. By doing so, the linear and gain properties of the JTWPA are extracted. Different factors that impact device performance including gain compression, phase matching, and fabrication imperfections are further investigated and modeled. A good agreement between simulation and measurements is identified, establishing the effectiveness of our approach in designing quantum parametric amplifiers.

titles.title: Designing Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers: EM-Circuit Cosimulation and Experimental Validation

abstracts.value: The q-plate is a spatially inhomogeneous SU(2) birefringent optical element that has garnered significant interest due to its ability to mediate the spin-orbit interaction of light and facilitate the generation of structured light with singularities. The q-plate features a spatially varying fast axis orientation defined by three parameters: the topological charge q, retardance delta, and the offset angle $alpha_0$. While the parameter alpha_0 can be changed many times by rotation, any change in the charge and/or retardance entails the fabrication of a new plate. This limitation can be overcome through the concept of an effective waveplate, where multiple waveplates, homogeneous or inhomogeneous, are aligned coaxially so that, under specific constraints, the composite system emulates the behavior of a single effective waveplate. This work presents a comprehensive mathematical formalism for realizing an effective waveplate through a cascaded configuration of three q-plates, each chosen as either a quarter-wave q-plate, a half-wave q-plate, or a combination thereof. Some configurations offer tunability of the retardance over the full range from 0 to $2pi$, even though q-plates with fixed retardances of $pi/2$ and pi are used in sequence to form an effective q-plate. This feature enables holonomic polarization walk on the higher-order Poincare sphere. Such a capability holds significant potential for applications involving structured light associated with the higher-order Poincare sphere, particularly in controlled polarization transformations and polarization-topology engineering.

titles.title: Mathematics of effective q-plate in polarization optics

abstracts.value: Quantum networked systems introduce a new class of threats that classical intrusion detection systems (IDS) were not designed to handle, as adversaries can manipulate quantum circuits at the gate, pulse, and measurement levels while also targeting the classical control plane by intercepting encrypted IDS communications for future decryption. This paper addresses this dual threat model by proposing a two-layer defense architecture that jointly secures both the quantum data plane and the IDS infrastructure. The first layer uses machine learning models trained on the Quantum Attack Dataset (QAD) to detect circuit-level attacks under both attack-balanced and heavily skewed class distributions. The second layer protects the IDS control plane with post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) primitives, specifically ML-KEM for key encapsulation and ML-DSA for authentication, mitigating exposure to future decryption attacks. Experimental results across multiple deployment conditions show that tree-based models achieve strong detection performance but degrade under class-prior shift, with pulse-level attacks remaining the most challenging to detect, highlighting limitations of current feature representations. To address this, a confidence-aware policy maps detections to monitoring, verification, and isolation actions, although the verification tier is rarely exercised under the evaluated distributions. The results show that detection and cryptographic protection must be designed together to achieve robust intrusion detection in quantum networked environments.

titles.title: PQC-Secured Intrusion Detection for Quantum Networks: A Two-Layer Defense Architecture

abstracts.value: Understanding the weak thermal links in supporting legs of transition edge sensors (TES) is crucial for developing highly sensitive bolometers used in cosmic microwave background detection. Conventional current-biased differential resistance measurements under varying temperature (R-T) are commonly used to characterize the resistance (R) and critical temperature (Tc) of TES. However, this method often encounters some phenomena: the bias current will affect the transition temperature obtained during Tb drop testing, as well as the obtained shape of the transition region. This behavior stems from the weak thermal links of TES under current bias, limiting R-T method to providing only rough information about the TES transition regime sometimes. The detailed and accurate performance parameters typically obtained via voltage-biased current-voltage I–V measurements using superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). In fact, the positive electro-thermal feedback induced by current bias contains valuable insights into the device’s intrinsic properties. This work focuses on elaborating the underlying mechanism: by analyzing the current-induced suppression of measured transition temperature in R-T measurements, we extract key parameters including thermal conductance (G), thermal exponent (n), Tc, and saturation power (Psat). This study provides intuitive calculations and visualizations of the electro-thermal behaviors induced by current bias in TES devices and offers a simple and rapid complementary tool for electro-thermal parameter extraction. For batch TES fabrication, it can serve as a pre-screening tool to improve the efficiency of subsequent high-precision SQUID-based I–V characterization.

titles.title: Unraveling Current-Bias-Induced Transition Discrepancy in Transition-Edge Sensors in R-T Tests and Establishing a Reliable Characterizing Method

abstracts.value: When constructing high-field magnets with nonmetallic formers, quench protection of slot-type magnets such as discrete-cosine-theta and canted-cosine-theta becomes particularly challenging, as nonmetallic structures cannot provide the quench-back effect. To address this issue, a 6+1 cable (six superconducting wires and one center cooper wire) configuration has been proposed. During a quench, the central copper strand acts as an internal heater, inducing the quench-back effect. However, the presence of the copper strand reduces the available slot space, thereby limiting the effective engineering current density. To further improve both the current density and protection performance, the coupling-loss induced quench (CLIQ) method has been introduced and applied to seven-strand superconducting cables without a central copper strand. In this study, an electro-thermal coupling model is employed to first validate, through experiment–simulation comparison, the effectiveness of quench-back protection in 6+1 cables. The same model is then extended to analyze and predict the quench protection performance of seven-strand cables under CLIQ. The results demonstrate that CLIQ can effectively trigger uniform quenching, significantly reducing the quench integral and hot-spot temperature, thereby ensuring the reliable protection of the magnet.

titles.title: Electro-Thermal Modeling of Quench-Back and CLIQ Protection for Multistrand Superconducting Magnets

abstracts.value: Superconducting transmon qubits form the backbone of today’s leading quantum processors, where high field dispersive readout relies fundamentally on the shape and temporal structure of microwave control pulses. While transmon qubits offer improved robustness against charge noise, their performance is still strongly influenced by environmental coupling, particularly the Purcell effect and by the spectral characteristics of the readout pulses used for state preparation and logic operations. In this article, we present a rigorous comparative analysis of qubit coherence dynamics using measurement under four relevant configurations: a single-step rectangular pulse without Purcell decay, a single-step pulse subject to Purcell-induced relaxation, a two-step shaped pulse without Purcell effects, and a two-step shaped pulse incorporating Purcell decay. By solving the time-dependent Lindblad master equation for a three-level transmon system, we illustrate how readout pulse shaping and Purcell filtering independently and jointly influence qubit population dynamics, excited-state lifetime, and the final-state fidelity. The results demonstrate that two-step readout pulse shaping significantly improves coherence by suppressing overshoot and reducing higher level population transfer, while the inclusion of Purcell mitigation further stabilizes the dynamics and enhances fidelity. The most notable observation is that the combined application of pulse shaping and Purcell filtering produces the most stable and highest fidelity qubit state discrimination. This unified perspective constitutes the central novelty of this article. Such a comparative framework, integrating pulse engineering with environmental decay modeling, has received limited explicit treatment in prior literature. The findings provide critical insights for optimizing both readout protocols and quantum hardware design in large-scale superconducting quantum systems.

titles.title: A Unified Open Quantum System Investigation of Leakage Suppressed Transmon Qubit Dynamics via Parametric Pulse Spectral Engineering, Purcell Limited Dissipation Control, and Dispersive Readout Phase Space Analysis

abstracts.value: The circular electron positron collider (CEPC) represents a major international scientific project, with its detector magnet proposing the use of the aluminum-stabilized stacked REBCO tapes cable (ASTC) in its high-temperature superconducting (HTS) design. To ensure the long-term stable and safe operation of this magnet, a thorough investigation on the quench behavior of the ASTC is imperative. This article presents a comprehensive 3-D quench simulation model for the ASTC, incorporating coupled electromagnetic-thermal analysis. The model is employed to simulate the global quench characteristics of the cable under liquid nitrogen immersion cooling, explicitly accounting for internal electrical contact resistance and thermal contact resistance. Key quench parameters, namely, the minimum quench energy (MQE) and quench propagation velocity (QPV), are investigated under varying operational currents, with particular emphasis on performance under adiabatic conditions representing the worst-case scenario. Simulation results demonstrate the significant role of the aluminum stabilizer in current sharing and heat conduction, contributing to the cable's stability and recoverability. The study confirms that the ASTC exhibits robust operational stability, where local quenches are unlikely to propagate into global quench events under effective cooling, thereby validating its suitability for the CEPC detector magnet application. The developed multiphysics model and simulation methodology provide a valuable framework for subsequent quench analysis of superconducting magnets.

titles.title: Study on Quench Behavior of Aluminum-Stabilized Stacked REBCO Tapes Cable

abstracts.value: Topological defects in two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) are canonical examples of generalized symmetries in quantum field theories. They not only encode key features of the underlying theory, but their study has also enhanced our understanding of renormalization group (RG) flows in theories that contain them. Lattice models exist which discretize the states, energy-momentum tensor, and primary fields of many 2D CFTs, raising the natural question of whether topological defects can be similarly discretized. In this thesis, we demonstrate that in many cases all topological defects of minimal model CFTs can be discretized, enabling analytical and ab-initio numerical computations of their properties. In some of these constructions, we make essential use of the integrable structure of the underlying lattice models. The lattice realization of these operators also permits the study of defect RG flows between CFTs with different topological defects inserted. These topological defects and defect RG flows are realized on the lattice not only for Hermitian but also for non-Hermitian lattice Hamiltonians. Studying topological defects in minimal model CFTs on the lattice has also opened the door to a deeper understanding of topological defects in CFTs where they remain poorly understood.

titles.title: Topological defects in conformal field theories and their lattice realizations

abstracts.value: The increasing use of robotic platforms in hazardous and magnetically complex environments, such as underground research facilities at CERN, demands a detailed understanding of how strong external magnetic fields affect electromechanical actuation. Quadruped robots equipped with electromagnetic (EM) motors are particularly vulnerable, as their actuators interact directly with ambient magnetic fluxes, generating additional mechanical forces and moments that can compromise stability, trajectory tracking and overall operational safety. This work presents a modeling framework for estimating the equivalent magnetic moment of an EM motor subjected to high-intensity magnetic fields. The proposed approach combines numerical simulation datasets with an analytical dipole-based formulation to derive a computationally efficient model capable of predicting magnetic-induced mechanical disturbances in real/time. The model accounts for the dependence of the magnetic moment on both the external field intensity and the motor’s orientation relative to the field lines, enabling the control system to anticipate disturbance torques and implement appropriate compensation strategies. The accuracy and reliability of the model were validated experimentally by rotating a Unitree GO-M8010-6 motor within controlled magnetic fields and comparing the measured torques with the model predictions. The results demonstrate close agreement in both trend and amplitude, confirming that the proposed formulation can provide the level of fidelity required for real-time control applications in magnetically harsh environments.

titles.title: Modeling mechanical disturbances induced by high intensity magnetic fields on electric motors

abstracts.value: A central theme of Physical Mathematics is that the partition function of a supersymmetric quantum field theory on a space $X$ often admits multiple interpretations, and the interplay between these viewpoints is a powerful source of new mathematical results. This thesis contributes to this dialogue in three directions, all within the framework of 4d $mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetry. In part I, we consider 5d $mathcal{N}=1$ $SU(2)$ super Yang-Mills theory on $X imes S^1$, with $X$ a closed smooth four-manifold. A partial topological twisting along $X$ renders the theory formally independent of the metric on $X$. The theory depends on the spin structure and the circumference $R$ of $S^1$. The coefficients of the $R$-expansion of the partition function are Witten indices, which are identified with $L^2$-indices of Dirac operators on moduli spaces of instantons. The partition function encodes BPS indices for instanton particles on a spatial manifold $X$, and these indices are special cases of K-theoretic Donaldson invariants. When the 't Hooft flux of the gauge theory is nonzero and $X$ is not spin, the 5d theory can be anomalous, but this anomaly can be canceled by coupling to a line bundle with connection for the global $U(1)$ "instanton number symmetry". For $b^+_2(X) > 0$ we derive the partition function from integration over the Coulomb branch of the effective 4d low-energy theory. When $X$ is toric we also use equivariant localization with respect to the $mathbb{C}^* imes mathbb{C}^*$ symmetry. The two methods lead to the same results for the wall-crossing formula. We also determine path integrals for four-manifolds with $b^+_2(X) > 1$. Our results agree with those for algebraic surfaces by Göttsche, Kool, Nakajima, Yoshioka, and Williams, but apply to a larger class of manifolds. When the circumference of the circle is tuned to special values, the path integral is associated with the 5d superconformal $E_1$ theory. Topological invariants in this case involve generalizations of Seiberg-Witten invariants. In part II, we relate the Macdonald index of a 4d $mathcal{N}=2$ SCFT to the Hilbert series of the arc space of the Zhu algebra of the corresponding Schur vertex operator algebra. Using this, we conjecture a simple closed-form formula for the Macdonald index of the $(A_1, D_{2n+1})$ Argyres-Douglas theories. We perform checks of the formula against the known Schur limits and RG flows. To match the Schur limit, we prove new $q$-series identities. Moreover, we propose a refinement of the Kontsevich-Soibelman wall-crossing operator for a class of 4d $mathcal{N}=2$ SCFTs whose Coulomb branch admits a source/sink chamber (a chamber in which the BPS quiver consists of only source and sink nodes) and whose nodes with valency greater than 2 are either all sources or all sinks. We present strong evidence that the trace of this refined operator computes the Macdonald index of the theory. In particular, we conjecture new closed-form expressions for the Macdonald indices of the $(A_1, mathfrak{g})$ Argyres-Douglas theories for any simply-laced Lie algebra $mathfrak{g}$.

abstracts.value: In recent decades, Quantum Computing (QC) has gained widespread attention among researchers and industries, driven by its potential to outperform classical systems in several key areas. However, validating novel quantum algorithms poses substantial challenges due to limited qubit availability and noise in current quantum devices. Although software simulators are frequently employed to validate quantum circuits, they are time-consuming and require high memory availability since as the number of qubits increases, the memory occupation grows exponentially. Hardware emulators have recently emerged as a faster, more efficient, cost-effective alternative. This article introduces AMARETTO (quAntuM ARchitecture EmulaTion TechnOlogy), a new architecture designed to improve quantum computing emulation on resource-constrained Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs). To provide a flexible and complete tool for quantum algorithm development, the emulator supports two universal gate sets, Clifford+T and rotational. AMARETTO mimics quantum computing’s inherent parallelism through multiple concurrent processing elements, achieving high throughput by harnessing the sparse nature of the gate matrices, coupled with pipelining in a Reduced Instruction Set Computer (RISC)-like architecture. A dedicated compiler translates OpenQASM 2.0 into AMARETTO’s instructions, enabling support for custom gates leveraging the equivalences known in the literature. Experimental results on an AMD Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC ZCU106 demonstrate successful emulation of quantum circuits up to eighteen qubits with a throughput of <inline-formula><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\mathbf{12.207}\frac{\mathbf{kgates}}{\mathbf{s}}$</tex-math></inline-formula>, validated against Qiskit simulators. Our evaluation confirms competitive performance with existing FPGA-based emulators in terms of throughput and scalability, while targeting an affordable FPGA platform.

titles.title: AMARETTO, Accelerating Quantum Algorithm Development With FPGA Emulation

abstracts.value: In 2021, Broadbent and Kazmi developed a gate-teleportation-based protocol for computational indistinguishability obfuscation of quantum circuits. This protocol is efficient for Clifford $+ {\textsf {T}}$ circuits with logarithmically many $\textsf {T}$ -gates, where the limiting factor in the efficiency of the protocol is the difficulty, on input a quantum circuit $C$ , of the classical task of producing a description of the unitary obtained by conjugating a Pauli $P$ (corresponding to a Bell-measurement outcome) by $C$ , where this description only depends on the input-output functionality of $CPC^{\dagger }$ . The task above, in turn, is at least as hard as the problem of determining whether two $n$ -qubit quantum circuits are perfectly equivalent up to global phase. In 2009, Tanaka defined the corresponding decision problem Exact Non-Identity Check (ENIC) and showed that ENIC is NQP-complete and thus NP-hard as well. Motivated by the 2021 protocol, we consider in this work what happens when we pass from low $\textsf {T}$ -count to low $\textsf {T}$ -depth. We show that, for Clifford $+ {\textsf {T}}$ -circuits of $\textsf {T}$ -depth $O(\log (n))$ , deciding ENIC remains NP-hard. In particular, we show this by relating certain decision problems on Pauli coefficients of Clifford $+ {\textsf {T}}$ unitaries to well-known hardness results for codeword weights in binary linear codes. This effectively rules out the possibility, for Clifford $+ {\textsf {T}}$ -circuits of logarithmic $\textsf {T}$ -depth, of either efficient ENIC or efficient gate-teleportation based computational indistinguishability obfuscation, unless $\text {P}=\text {NP}$ . It also provides a new, independent proof of the hardness of ENIC, even at low $\textsf {T}$ -depth. Along the way, we prove the NP-hardness of some related circuit problems.

titles.title: Exact Non-Identity Check and Gate-Teleportation-Based Indistinguishability Obfuscation Are NP-Hard for Low---Depth Quantum Circuits

abstracts.value: Divisible codes have been studied for many years, since the divisibility theorem on binary cyclic codes was proved by R. J. McEliece in 1972 and divisible codes were introduced by H. N. Ward in 1981. It is well-known that doubly even (4-divisible) binary codes can be used to construct stabilizer quantum codes. Triorthogonal binary codes and CSS-T pairs of binary codes were introduced to construct CSS-T quantum codes. In this paper, we show that 8-divisible (triply even) binary linear codes are triorthogonal codes and CSS-T pairs of codes can be obtained from 8-divisible codes directly. Infinitely many infinite families of <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$2^{r}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>-divisible optimal binary codes are presented, for an arbitrarily large positive integer <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$r$ </tex-math></inline-formula>. Seventeen doubly even (self-orthogonal) binary cyclic codes and five triply even binary cyclic codes with their minimum weights equal to the minimum weights of best-known linear codes are found. An infinite family of rate around <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\frac {1}{2}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> explicit doubly even (self-orthogonal) binary cyclic codes with the lower bound <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\frac {n_{i}}{\log n_{i}}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> on their minimum distances and the lower bound <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sqrt {\frac {n_{i}}{2}}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> on their dual distances is constructed. This is much stronger than the main results in two previous papers published in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2022 and 2024 by C. Ding, C. Tang, Z. Sun and C. Li. Many CSS-T quantum codes with new parameters are constructed. Many stabilizer quantum codes given in this paper have distances close to the best-known ones documented in Grassl’s database.

titles.title: Optimal, Best-Known Divisible Binary Codes and Related Quantum Codes

abstracts.value: A quantum message is encoded into <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N$ </tex-math></inline-formula> quantum storage systems <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$Q_{1} {\dots } Q_{N}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> with assistance from <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N_{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> maximally entangled bi-partite quantum systems <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$A_{1}B_{1}, {\dots }, A_{N_{B}}B_{N_{B}}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>, that are prepared in advance such that <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$B_{1} {\dots } B_{N_{B}}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> are stored separately as entanglement assistance (EA) systems, while <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$A_{1} {\dots } A_{N_{B}}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> are made available to the encoder. Both the storage systems and EA systems are erasure-prone. The quantum message must be recoverable given any <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$K$ </tex-math></inline-formula> of the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N$ </tex-math></inline-formula> storage systems along with any <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$K_{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> of the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N_{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> EA systems. The capacity for this setting is the maximum size of the quantum message, given that the size of each EA system is <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\lambda _{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula>. All system sizes are relative to the size of a storage system, which is normalized to unity. The exact capacity is characterized as a function of <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N,K,N_{B},K_{B}, \lambda _{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> in all cases, with one exception. The capacity remains open for an intermediate range of <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\lambda _{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> values when a strict majority of the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N$ </tex-math></inline-formula> storage systems, and a strict non-zero minority of the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"> <tex-math notation="LaTeX">$N_{B}$ </tex-math></inline-formula> EA systems, are erased. For the open regime, we conjecture that our inner (achievability) bound is tight. As a key stepping stone, an analogous classical storage (with shared-randomness assistance) problem is introduced. A set of constraints is identified for the classical problem, including that the classical storage systems can recover the shared-randomness in particular, such that classical linear code constructions translate to quantum storage codes, and the converse bounds for the two settings utilize similar insights. In particular, the capacity characterizations for the classical and quantum settings are shown to be identical in all cases where the capacity is settled.

titles.title: On the Capacity of Erasure-Prone Quantum Storage With Erasure-Prone Entanglement Assistance

abstracts.value: With the evolution of 5G X-haul connections and the emergence of new infrastructure segments, the need for efficient multiplexing schemes is paramount to support secure quantum communications alongside classical traffic. This study addresses this need by demonstrating successful coexistence of QKD and 5G services over existing X-haul infrastructure, with simultaneous transmission of 10 Gb/s classical data alongside C-band single photons, achieving raw click rates of 4.3 kbps and 51.9 kbps over 22.6 km backhaul (BH) and 2.2 km fronthaul (FH) fiber links, respectively. We introduce a practical multiplexing scheme based on high-isolation, fiber-based filters and multiplexers, enabling the seamless integration of the QKD transmitter and receiver into both BH and FH links without modifying the existing X-haul infrastructure. Experimental results demonstrate continuous and stable operation achieving average QBER values of 4.7% and 2.6%, yielding calculated Secret Key Rates (SKRs) of 650 bps and 6.8 kbps for quantum-secured BH and FH links, respectively, while also maintaining uninterrupted 5G service. Finally, it is investigated whether these SKR are sufficient to meet the requirements for AES-256 encryption for securing the X-haul data exchange. This work provides a practical approach to integrating QKD within deployed 5G X-haul connections, supporting future quantum-secured mobile communications.

titles.title: Integration of C-Band Polarization-Encoded QKD Over Deployed 5G X-Haul Infrastructure

abstracts.value: This article presents the design of a four-channel front-end application specific integrated circuit (ASIC), ATLAS liquid argon front-end (ALFE), developed for the readout of the liquid-argon calorimeter (LAr) detector in the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). ALFE enables the readout of current signals induced in the LAr with a dynamic range (DR) exceeding 16 bits, while ensuring seamless operation in a system comprising nearly 200000 channels with detector capacitances ranging from 0.16 to 2 nF per channel. Each analog front-end (AFE) channel provides configurable and matched input impedance of either 50 or $25~\Omega $ , measures an equivalent noise current (ENI) of $\mathbf {47.5}$ or $\mathbf {147.5~\text {nA}}$ , achieves sub- $\mathbf {0.2\% }$ integral non-linearity (INL) for signal peak measurement, and maintains a power supply rejection (PSR) exceeding 14 dB up to $\mathbf {1~\text {MHz}}$ . Each AFE channel incorporates a low-noise amplifier (LNA) with a noise figure (NF) of 0.5 or 0.95 dB and an input-referred voltage noise density of $ \mathbf {0.28~\text {nV}/(\text {Hz})^{1/2} }$ . This LNA is implemented with a fully-differential amplifier (FDA) enclosed in an asymmetric differential feedback (ADF), followed by a two-gain fully differential CR–RC2 bandpass filter (BPF). ALFE can withstand a radiation-induced total ionizing dose (TID) exceeding 1.4 Mrad. Besides the four AFE channels, ALFE integrates an analog trigger-sum (ATS), an SEE/SEU-tolerant I2C interface, voltage and current references, and current digital-to-analog converters (DACs).

titles.title: A 0.5-/0.95-dB NF, 50-/25-$\Omega$ Configurable CMOS Front-End ASIC for the Readout of Liquid Argon Calorimeter in the LHC

abstracts.value: Current gravitational-wave (GW) detectors face fundamental sensitivity limits below 10 Hz, driven largely by low-frequency seismic noise. Achieving effective isolation across complex GW instruments is a challenging experimental and control problem due to multi-subsystem coupling, tilt-to-translation coupling, and nonlinear interactions between ground motion and active control loops. This thesis addresses these limitations by unifying optimal control design framework.To streamline optimization in high-dimensional systems, a novel multi-scale optimal control framework is introduced. The method employs a fundamental control-loop suppression limit—defined as an "acausal optimum" curve—to assess global optimality and simplify control synthesis. This approach is applied to candidate active seismic isolation platforms for the Einstein Telescope (ET), including OmniSens. OmniSens is a novel 6-degree-of-freedom active seismic isolation system utilizing a low-loss pendulum with interferometric sensors. This demonstrates the ability to optimize models with dozens of coupled state variables simultaneously.The commissioning of OmniSens is detailed through the characterization of its sensors, actuators, and electronics, experimentally validating the low-complexity mathematical models developed earlier for the platform. Systematic calibration, actuator tuning to minimize cross-couplings, and open-loop transfer function measurements demonstrate strong agreement between physical laboratory results and models.Finally, the thesis critically evaluates standard Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) and Gaussian assumptions by reframing seismic isolation as a prediction problem, paving the way for future non-LTI control techniques. Together, these theoretical frameworks, modeling tools, and experimental validations provide key technical building blocks to enable target low-frequency sensitivity in next-generation detectors like the Einstein Telescope.

titles.title: Optimal Control for Einstein Telescope

abstracts.value: <jats:p>Pseudo-Schouten symmetric spacetimes are examined under a differential condition on the Schouten tensor, producing explicit relations for the scalar curvature, the Ricci tensor, and the associated covector field. It is shown that the associated covector is a Ricci eigenvector and is irrotational, acceleration-free, and vorticity-free. Corresponding reductions of the Ricci tensor are obtained, including perfect fluid forms under suitable conditions. Ricci recurrent and Ricci semi-symmetric cases are also considered, leading to further curvature restrictions and compatibility properties involving the Riemann and Weyl tensors. In vacuum [Formula: see text]-gravity, the Ricci tensor is decomposed into a perfect fluid part and an anisotropic term governed by the shear tensor, equivalently by the electric part of the Weyl tensor. A comoving frame analysis shows that the shear vanishes, so that the associated covector is torse-forming and the spacetime reduces to a generalized Robertson–Walker model, and in four dimensions to a Robertson–Walker spacetime. Moreover, the Weyl tensor is divergence-free and annihilated by the associated covector. These results give a geometric characterization of pseudo-Schouten symmetric spacetimes in both the general setting and the vacuum [Formula: see text]-gravity case.</jats:p>

titles.title: Investigations of pseudo-shouten symmetric spacetimes in f(R)-gravity vacuum solutions

Summary

English:
Charged lepton flavour violation (cLFV) is a clear sign of physics beyond the Standard Model
(SM) and has not yet been observed experimentally. Future experiments like Mu2e or COMET
aim to improve the sensitivity to cLFV observables by several orders of magnitude, sparking
interest in models which can generate experimentally accessible branching ratios for such ob-
servables. The class of vector-like lepton (VLL) models, extending the SM by one or more gen-
erations of vector-like lepton multiplets, is able to generate experimentally accessible branching
ratios for cLFV observables. This thesis analyzes in detail the parameter space of one par-
ticular VLL model, which extends the SM by a VLL singlet and doublet. The focus is laid
upon cLFV observables, such as muon conversions in nuclei and muon decays to electrons
and photons. It is shown that this VLL model has wide and consistent parameter spaces in
which cLFV observables can be generated by various different mechanisms and contributions,
that go beyond what would be expected in models with dipole dominance. Various different
dominance and clustering regimes are identified, demonstrating the versatility of the model’s
parameter space. It is furthermore shown that the parameter space allows for experimentally
accessible branching ratios for muon conversions in nuclei as well as muon decays to electrons
and photons, while still being consistent with all other experimental constraints, without the
need for large finetuning or strongly hierarchical couplings.

Deutsch:
Lepton-Flavour verletzende Observablen sind ein eindeutiges Anzeichen für Physik jenseits
des Standardmodells (SM) und wurden experimentell bisher nicht beobachtet. Zukünftige Ex-
perimente wie Mu2e oder COMET zielen darauf ab, die Sensitivität für cLFV-Observablen
um mehrere Größenordnungen zu verbessern, was das Interesse an Modellen weckt, die ex-
perimentell zugängliche Zerfallsraten für solche Observablen erzeugen können. Die Klasse der
vektorartigen Leptonmodelle (VLL), die das SM um eine oder mehrere Generationen vek-
torieller koppelnder Lepton-Multipletts erweitern, ist in der Lage, experimentell zugängliche
Zerfallsraten für cLFV-Observablen zu erzeugen. Diese Arbeit analysiert den Parameterraum
eines bestimmten VLL-Modells, welches das SM um ein VLL-Singlett und ein VLL-Doublett
erweitert. Der Fokus liegt auf cLFV-Observablen wie Myon-Umwandlungen in Kernen und
Myon-Zerfällen zu Elektronen und Photonen. Es wird gezeigt, dass dieses VLL-Modell weite
und konsistente Parameterbereiche besitzt, in denen cLFV-Observablen durch verschiedene
Mechanismen und Beiträge erzeugt werden können, die über Dipol-Dominanz hinausgehen.
Verschiedene Dominanz- und Clusterregime werden identifiziert, was die Vielseitigkeit des Pa-
rameterraums des Modells demonstriert. Es wird außerdem gezeigt, dass der Parameterraum
experimentell zugängliche Zerfallsraten für Myon-Umwandlungen in Kernen erlaubt, während
alle experimentellen Einschränkungen eingehalten werden, ohne dass dafür starke Feinabstim-
mungen oder stark hierarchische Kopplungsstrukturen notwendig wären.

1 Motivation and Thesis
Overview

The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics is one of the most successful theories in physics,
describing all known matter content and three of their four fundamental interactions. Observ-
ables which are predicted by the SM, like the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron
Δ𝑎𝑒, are tested up to accuracies exceeding 1 parts per trillion (Fan et al. [1]). However, with
our current understanding of the SM, there are still many open questions, such as the nature
and origin of dark matter, the origin of neutrino masses, or the inclusion and UV-completion
of gravity in the preexisting framework of quantum field theories.
Many different variants of beyond SM (BSM) theories have been proposed to explain these
open questions. These extensions contain classes of new physics models like supersymme-
try (SUSY), which exploits subtleties in the Coleman-Mandula theorem and extends the SM
through supersymmetric fields, or grand unified theories (GUTs) like 𝐸6 that often extend the
SM with a large set of new gauge and matter fields, unifying the interactions of the SM at a
large GUT energy scale. In many of those, like some GUT theories but also eg. composite
Higgs models, the chiral SM fermion fields are supplemented with new vectorially coupling
fermion fields. While chiral lepton family extensions of the SM which couple exactly as the
other three generations are heavily constrained (Janot and Jadach [2]; Barducci et al. [3]),
the much more unrestricted parameter space of vector-like lepton (VLL) family extensions
can still offer a wide variety of implications for new physics scenarios. The phenomenology of
these VLLs is the main focus of this thesis, especially in the context of charged lepton-flavour
violating (cLFV) observables.
One such cLFV observable is the neutrinoless decay of muons into electrons. In the minimal
SM without neutrino masses there is no cLFV at any loop order and any such observable
branching ratio (BR) is vanishing. Since neutrinos are observed to be massive particles we
have to extend the SM by a neutrino mass generation mechanism. Because of the additional
effect of neutrino mixing we then also have nonzero but extremely suppressed cLFV BRs,
proportional to ℬℛ(𝜇 → 𝑒𝛾) ∝

The goal of this thesis is to study one specific VLL model, calculate cLFV observables and

The SM is a (3+1) dimensional relativistic quantum field theory that describes the elec-
tromagnetic, weak, and strong nuclear interactions. Before spontaneous symmetry break-
ing (SSB) of the electroweak sector the SM is a gauge theory described by the gauge group
𝑆𝑈(3)𝐶 ⊗ 𝑆𝑈(2)𝐿 ⊗ 𝑈(1)𝑌 and the interactions between its matter content are derived from
the principle of local gauge invariance. After SSB, the electroweak symmetry is broken to
the electromagnetic 𝑈(1)𝑄 gauge group, giving mass to the weak gauge bosons and fermions
through the Higgs mechanism, resulting in another gauge theory described by the gauge group
𝑆𝑈(3)𝐶 ⊗ 𝑈(1)𝑄.

2.1 SM Particle Content
The field content can be classified into fermionic and bosonic particles, according to their
spin. Before SSB, the massless spin-1 𝑈(1)𝑌 boson 𝐵, the three 𝑆𝑈(2)𝐿 bosons 𝑊 𝑎, and
eight 𝑆𝑈(3)𝐶 bosons 𝑔𝑎, called gluons, mediate three of the four known fundamental forces
of nature described by the SM. The Higgs 𝑆𝑈(2) doublet 𝐻 is a scalar field with a specific
potential 𝑉 , whose shape causes the spontaneous symmetry breaking of the electroweak sector.
After SSB the 𝑈(1)𝑌 and 𝑆𝑈(2)𝐿 bosons mix to form the massless photon 𝛾 and the massive
𝑊± and 𝑍 bosons. The photon then mediates an interaction corresponding to an unbroken
electromagnetic 𝑈(1)𝑄 interaction between electrically charged particles. The eight massless
gluons are 𝑆𝑈(3)𝐶 gauge bosons that mediate the strong interaction between colour-charged
particles, which includes the gluons themselves, introducing a first instance of self-interactions

symmetry, the 𝑊± and 𝑍 vector bosons. The weak interaction is unique in the SM, since it
does not conserve charge-parity (CP) symmetry, coupling only to left-handed particles and
right-handed anti-particles. Finally, the scalar Higgs boson ℎ is the physical remnant of the
Higgs doublet after SSB. The Higgs boson couples to all massive particles and is responsible
for generating their masses through the Higgs mechanism, which will be discussed in more

2.3 Flavour Physics in the SM
Between generations, the SM fermions can only be distinguished by their masses. To character-
ize this difference and describe transitions between particles the term ”flavour” is introduced.
In the SM there are six flavours of quarks and six flavours of leptons, grouped into three
generations as shown in Table 2.3.

2.3.1 Mass Eigenstates
Since differently flavoured particles of same gauge quantum numbers in different generations
only differ by their mass, the origin of these fermion mass terms is of particular interest for
understanding the dynamics of intergenerational flavour transitions. As shown in the previous
section, the mass terms are generated through the Yukawa interactions after SSB. The Yukawa
matrices 𝑦𝑢,𝑑,𝑒 are in general non-diagonal complex matrices and must be diagonalized to obtain
physical masses and their corresponding mass eigenstates. It is useful to consider a simplified
Lagrangian of the form

ℒ = 𝑖𝐹𝐿𝑖/𝜕𝐹𝐿𝑖 + 𝑖𝑓𝑅𝑗 /𝜕𝑓𝑅𝑗 − 𝑣 𝐹𝐿𝑖𝑌𝑖𝑗𝑓𝑅𝑗 + ℎ.𝑐. (2.26)

which would, for example, be obtained from the leptonic part of the Lagrangian after SSB,
ignoring the Higgs and gauge interactions. The kinetic terms of this Lagrangian are invariant
under transformation with chiral unitary diagonalization matrices 𝑈𝐿 and 𝑈𝑅 on the flavour
space

𝐹𝐿 → 𝑈𝐿𝐹𝐿 (2.27a)

𝑓𝑅 → 𝑈𝑅𝑓𝑅. (2.27b)

With the appropriate choice of 𝑈𝐿 and 𝑈𝑅, the Yukawa matrix 𝑌 can then be diagonalized.
This procedure is equivalent to a singular value decomposition (SVD) of the Yukawa ma-
trix. The resulting diagonal matrix 𝑌𝐷 contains the physical Yukawa couplings, which are
proportional to the physical fermion masses. The fields in this new basis are called mass
eigenstates, while the original fields are called flavour eigenstates. In a more general theory,
all two-point functions are diagonalized in a similar way so that the physical masses, used to
define propagators, and the corresponding mass eigenstates are obtained.

2.3.2 Interactions in the Mass Basis
While the kinetic terms are invariant under these chiral transformations of Equation (2.27),
the interaction terms in the Lagrangian are generally not. This is especially important for the
electroweak interactions, where 𝑊 interactions are non-diagonal in chiral and Higgs interac-
tions in flavour space.
As an example, a toy model with two fermions 𝐹 = (𝑓1 𝑓2), whose masses are generated by a
non-diagonal Yukawa matrix 𝑌 , is considered. Interaction with a gauge boson 𝐴 with different
quantum numbers 𝑡𝐴 1/2 for both fermions 𝑓1/2 is assumed, such that the flavour eigenstates
give eigenvalues

𝑇𝐴𝐹 = (𝑇𝐴𝑓1 𝑇𝐴𝑓2) = (𝑡𝐴2𝑓1 𝑡𝐴1𝑓2) := 𝑡𝐴𝐹 (2.28)

with 𝑡𝐴 as a diagonal matrix containing the quantum numbers of the fermions under the gauge
interaction 𝐴. The interaction terms in the Lagrangian then reads

ℒ ⊃ 𝑔𝐴𝐹 /𝐴𝑡𝐴𝐹. (2.29)

In the mass eigenstate basis 𝐹 → 𝑈𝐹 , this transforms to

ℒ ⊃ 𝑔𝐴𝐹 /𝐴(𝑈 †𝑡𝐴𝑈)𝐹. (2.30)

If the quantum number matrices 𝑡𝐴 are not proportional to the identity matrix, they generally
do not commute with the diagonalization matrices. This will lead to non-diagonal interaction
matrices in the mass basis, allowing for flavour changing neutral currents (FCNCs) mediated
by the 𝐴 boson with transition strengths proportional to the off-diagonal elements of 𝑈 †𝑡𝐴𝑈 .
In the SM, FCNCs cannot be written down at tree level, since all fermions with off-diagonal

3.5 cLFV Feynman Rules
To obtain Feynman rules of physically measurable parameters we have to solve the SVD of
the mass Matrix ℳ. There are a handful of caveats that complicate this ordeal significantly.
Firstly, to solve for the SVD matrices, even in cases of a minimal nonzero set of parameters
that would be necessary for cLFV, it is necessary to solve for the roots of polynomials of degree
at least 5, making a general analytic solution impossible. Secondly, the physical masses, which
correspond to the singular values of the various mass matrices, are in itself input parameters,
while the Yukawa couplings inside the matrices are not. This problem can be reduced to an
inverse eigenvalue or singular value problem (IEP, ISVP), where a parameterized operator, in
our case the mass matrix, has its parameters adjusted such that the spectrum of the operator
matches a given set of eigenvalues , in our case the physical masses of the charged SM leptons
(Chu and Golub [12]; Kern [13]).
In this thesis two different approaches were used to solve for the SVD matrices and, ultimately,
the Feynman rules used for the calculations of the observables. The first approach uses a
pertrubative expansion in small couplings

4 Observables
With the Feynman rules defined, the observables that constrain the VLL model are now con-
sidered. The main focus of this thesis is placed on experiments in which a muon is converted
into an electron in the presence of a nucleus, and possible parameter spaces in which the
VLL model could contribute to this cLFV process are constrained. Such measurements are
performed by the SINDRIUM II experiment (SINDRUM II Collaboration [15]) or the upcom-
ing experiments COMET (COMET Collaboration [16]) and Mu2e (Mu2e Collaboration [17]),
where gold or aluminium nuclei are used as targets, respectively, and muons are converted to
electrons in their nucleon field.
To constrain the wide, 10-dimensional parameter space of the VLL model, other observables
that are either sensitive to cLFV processes or receive corrections through interactions of the
new fields in the VLL model are also considered.

4.1 Effective Operators and Wilson Coefficients
Most of the observables of interest can be described within an effective field theory (EFT)
framework. In this approach, all heavy degrees of freedom are integrated out, and the low-
energy effects are described through a set of effective operators 𝒪𝑖 of fixed mass dimension 𝑑

and their corresponding Wilson coefficients 𝐶𝑖. To provide general results, coefficient matching
onto the WET-3 basis (Jenkins et al. [18]) is performed, which is widely used as a general basis
for low-energy EFTs containing operators with mass dimension 𝑑 ≤ 6. The translation from
the WET-3 basis to other low-energy effective Lagrangians is then straightforward and mostly
involves a linear combination of operators to obtain the Lagrangian required for a specific
observable. One such effective Lagrangian is given by

4.6 Quartic Higgs Coupling and Vacuum
Stability

A more indirect constraint on the VLL parameter space is derived from the requirement of vac-
uum stability. The presence of VLLs and their couplings to the Higgs can significantly modify
the running of the quartic Higgs coupling 𝜆𝐻 from low to high energy scales. To generate a
stable vacuum, the quartic higgs coupling must remain positive at all energy scales up to a
desired energy scale, which ideally would be the GUT or Planck scale. In the SM, the vacuum
is meta-stable and near criticality Degrassi et al. [37], meaning that within uncertainties of
the parameters used in the matching and depending on the scale up to which the coupling is
run, the SM vacuum can exhibit both stable as well as unstable parameter configurations.

like analyticity, especially within interative root-finding algorithms. Trying to circumvent
converging to a solution which is not consistent with analyticity could entail using a more
sophisticated method of initial guessing. This however is highly difficult since it involves
accounting for parameter spaces in which fine-tuning and large cancellations are necessary to
get mass singular values and would basically amount to guessing the correct Yukawa coupling
from the start, which is not feasible. This approach was therefore neglected in favor of an
easier method that does not require a sophisticated initial guess by circumventing the sorting
problem, giving, at least for this use case, the expected analytic results. Instead of looking
at the possibly nonsquare matrices ℳ which need to be SVDd, the square matrix ℳ†ℳ is
considered, and diagonalization is used to get the eigenvalues corresponding to the squared
singular values. This then gives a clear characteristic polynomial with which the root finding
algorithm can be applied without sorting issues because the ordering can be imposed from
the start instead of sorting the eigenvalues by size in every root-finding iteration step. This
algorithm has been implemented in Mathematica and uses the built-in FindRoot function. The
resulting Yukawa parameters 𝑦𝑖 are used to calculate the SVD matrices 𝑈𝐿/𝑅 and the mass
matrix ℳ numerically, given a set machine precision. Similar issues also arise in other contexts,
e.g., while determining SUSY parameters during renormalization group running between low
and high scales. Different approaches to solve these issues exist in spectrum generators like
FlexibleSUSY (Athron et al. [41]) from which ideas could be adapted in the future, should
current approaches falter. With this, a consistently ordered solution set 𝑦 is obtained, with
which the SVD can be carried out such that the proposed singular values are achieved.

7 Conclusion and Outlook
The studied VLL model, extending the SM by one generation of singlet and doublet VLLs,
has a vast and versatile parameter space, which allows cLFV observables to be induced by
various different mechanisms and contributions. The model is able to produce experimentally
accessible branching ratios for muon conversions in nuclei as well as muon decays to electrons
and photons, which go beyond the set ratios predicted in models with dipole dominance.
Mutliple different dominance and clustering regimes can be seen, in which ℬℛ(𝜇𝑁 → 𝑒𝑁)

and ℬℛ(𝜇 → 3𝑒) can be consistently larger than ℬℛ(𝜇 → 𝑒𝛾) by several orders of magnitude,
showing that non-dipole contributions can play a significant role in generating cLFV in this
model. It is seen that in most conceivable parameter configurations, in which cLFV is possible,
the parameter space is constrained by electroweak precision observables as well as as current
cLFV limits. Dipole or Higgs coupling constraints, like AMMs or Higgs decays to leptons,
can be circumvented by choosing parameter configurations, in which the leading contributions
vanish. Such configurations include vanishing 𝜆 couplings or imposing strong hierarchical
structures, in which one lepton couples to the doublet VLL and the other to the singlet
VLL only. This work especially shows that, should future experiments observe cLFV in muon
conversion or muon decays, this model could provide a viable explanation for such observations,
while still being consistent with all other experimental constraints, without the need for large
finetuning or strongly hierarchical couplings.
Future analyses of this model should include setting explicit constraints on the parameter
space from electroweak precision observables, similarly to what has already been done for
purely muonic couplings (Möhling et al. [14]; Dermisek and Raval [11]). Another point which
should be expanded upon, are chirally non-enhanced contributions to form factors, which have
not been calculated consistently in this thesis. While these contributions are expected to be
subdominant in most of the parameter space, in cases of strong cancellations and sign flips of
non-positive observables, these contributions could become relevant. Furthermore, the vacuum
stability of the model should be analyzed in more detail and at higher loop level. With this it
might be possible to strongly constrain the allowed parameter space, especially in regions where
masses and couplings become large, giving stringent constraints on when the model remains
perturbative and stable up to high energy scales. Concerning the numerical implementation
of the model, the numerical stability of the Yukawa parameter Inversion algorithm has to be
studied further to ensure consistent results, which follow analyticity conditions.

abstracts.value:
Charged lepton flavour violation (cLFV) is a clear sign of physics beyond the Standard Model
(SM) and has not yet been observed experimentally. Future experiments like Mu2e or COMET
aim to improve the sensitivity to cLFV observables by several orders of magnitude, sparking
interest in models which can generate experimentally accessible branching ratios for such ob
servables. The class of vector-like lepton (VLL) models, extending the SM by one or more gen
erations of vector-like lepton multiplets, is able to generate experimentally accessible branching
ratios for cLFV observables. This thesis analyzes in detail the parameter space of one par
ticular VLL model, which extends the SM by a VLL singlet and doublet. The focus is laid
upon cLFV observables, such as muon conversions in nuclei and muon decays to electrons
and photons. It is shown that this VLL model has wide and consistent parameter spaces in
which cLFV observables can be generated by various different mechanisms and contributions,
that go beyond what would be expected in models with dipole dominance. Various different
dominance and clustering regimes are identified, demonstrating the versatility of the model’s
parameter space. It is furthermore shown that the parameter space allows for experimentally
accessible branching ratios for muon conversions in nuclei as well as muon decays to electrons
and photons, while still being consistent with all other experimental constraints, without the
need for large finetuning or strongly hierarchical couplings.

titles.title: Phenomenology of the Vector-like Lepton Model for Lepton-flavour Violating Observables

The HEP software community has identified scalability, complexity, and cost as barriers to advancing high-performance computing in high-energy physics. We intend to address these issues by pulling technology from other domains, such as artificial intelligence, traditional financial technology, web3, and blockchain. By combining computational systems from other domains with existing HEP software, the HEP software community can share costs, pool resources, and aggregate computation power with other computational domains addressing these issues.

In this talk, we will describe the current status and design of our blockchain system which leverages existing open source software technology and web3 for generalized high-performance computing and its application to high energy physics and AI. Our computational infrastructure using comprises a decentralized blockchain system that passes messages between computational nodes, implemented as docker/OCI containers. We use an the end-to-end principle to place policy controls at the endpoints, drastically simplifying computational complexity and removing barriers to international resource sharing between institutions and professional domains.

To support HEP workflows, we are integrating the streaming network with a computational node that uses the Key4Hep framework to include software commonly used in HEP, such as ROOT, Gaudi, and Podio. We have designed the system to allow easy integration with software-as-a-service systems such as AI providers such as ChatGPT or OpenLllama. We have designed the system to be scalable both upward, allowing the creation of computational networks of the scale of the Bitcoin computation network, and downward, allowing the creation of simple ad hoc distributed computation systems. An open-source prototype of our work is available on GitHub, and we are seeking users and developers from the HEP community.

titles.title: Applications Of Blockchain Technology To Distributed Computing In High Energy Physics

ii



Author’s Declaration

This thesis consists of material all of which I authored or co-authored: see Statement
of Contributions included in the thesis. This is a true copy of the thesis, including any
required final revisions, as accepted by my examiners. I understand that my thesis may be
made electronically available to the public.

iii



Statement of Contributions

The thesis contains two parts (see Outline 1.4).

Part I is based on a short paper [1] that has been written in collaboration with Matthew
Fox (University of Colorado, Boulder) and Chaitanya Karamchedu (University of Mary-
land). This project was born several years ago with Matthew, during our Master’s year
at the Perimeter Scholar’s International (PSI) program in 2021-2022. Matthew attended
a talk at Perimeter on the Schrödinger-Newton equation and its foundations, while I was
working on a winter school project on collapse models based on that equation (with Latham
Boyle). We soon realized that Matthew’s interest in computational complexity theory and
mine in gravitational physics could lead to an interesting project, so we started working to-
gether. It was not until 2024-2025, though, that we were able to convert our original ideas
into something more concrete. Teamed up with our friend Chai, we wrote an essay for the
2026 Gravity Research Foundation Essay Competition. This evolved into a paper, which is
currently under review at Physical Review Letters (PRL) (submitted June 24, 2026). All
authors contributed equally to the writing of the paper and the conceptualization of the
ideas. The most important difference in Part I from the paper [1] is that the introduction
(Chapter 2) is slightly more expanded here, and we added three figures.

Part II is based on a considerably longer paper [2] that I co-authored with my PhD
supervisor Latham Boyle (Higgs Centre for Theoretical Physics, University of Edinburgh
and Perimeter Institute). The project started in 2022 in my PSI Master’s Essay, where
we mentioned the first speculations about how a Lorentzian quasicrystal – if it existed –
could be relevant for string theory compactifications. Building these quasicrystals math-
ematically and understanding their properties has been the main part of my PhD work
since then. While Part II contains the paper [2], it is a substantial extension of that work
in the following sense:

• The introduction in Chapter 6 has been expanded from the paper, especially the
part referring to Coxeter’s theory; there are more figures here and more thorough
explanations.

• Chapter 8 has been revised as well, especially the parts about the non-crystallographic
symmetries in Sections 8.1 and 8.2. I added more figures throughout and another
example of a spacetime quasicrystal in Section 8.4.

• Chapters 9 and 11 are entirely new and are based on ongoing unpublished work
that I have been doing on my own since April 2026. This thesis is the first time

iv



that these ideas are reported, apart from Lemma 1 in Appendix B and the related
discussion in Section 9.1 that was worked out by Alex Thorne [3] in a Master’s
thesis at the University of Edinburgh, for which I served as the co-supervisor (with
Latham Boyle). I acknowledge useful discussions with Latham Boyle and Yasaman
Yazdi (Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies) for the content of these chapters, and
especially with Alex Thorne (see Acknowledgements)

• All the appendices, apart from Section A.3 and Appendix D that were copied from our
paper [2] have been written from scratch for this thesis. Appendix B, in particular,
might be of independent mathematical interest.

Other minor revisions have been carried out throughout the thesis. At the time of writing,
the paper [2] is peer review at Physical Review Research (PRR) (submitted February 24,
2026), and we are expecting the first referee report. More publications are to follow from
the new results of this thesis.

Unless otherwise stated, all figures in this thesis have been produced by me, either in
Mathematica or by drawing them by hand on my reMarkable tablet.

Finally, I have been heavily benefited from interactions with Anthropic’s Claude Code,
who helped me drastically revise my own code and build more efficient new functions,
especially for the new results of Chapter 11. I have also used Google’s Gemini quite
frequently for browsing through the literature, and as a research assistant (using the Pro
Extended version), to bounce ideas off of.

v



Abstract

Part I: Semiclassical Gravity Efficiently Solves NP-Complete Problems

Assuming the gravitational field is classical and that it couples to quantum fields via the
semiclassical Einstein field equations, we show that the weak-field dynamics of a massive
and non-relativistic qubit can in principle be used to solve an NP-complete problem in
polynomial time. We attribute this vast computational power to the non-linear qubit
dynamics afforded by the semiclassical Einstein field equations. Consequently, the above
two assumptions entail a violation of the Physical Extended Church–Turing Thesis, which
we regard as evidence for the quantization of gravity.

Part II: Spacetime Quasicrystals

Self-similar quasicrystals (like the famous Penrose and Ammann-Beenker tilings) are
exceptional geometric structures in which long-range order, quasi-periodicity, non crystal-
lographic orientational symmetry, and discrete scale invariance are tightly interwoven in a
beautiful way. Here, we show how such structures may be generalized from Euclidean space
to Minkowski spacetime. We construct the first examples of such Lorentzian quasicrystals
(the spacetime analogues of the Penrose or Ammann-Beenker tilings), and point out key
novel features of these structures (compared to their Euclidean cousins). Then, we present
some ideas about how such spacetime quasicrystals might relate to reality.

First, we mention a speculative yet intriguing scenario in which our infinite (3 + 1)D
universe is embedded (like one of our spacetime quasicrystal examples) in a particularly
symmetric (9 + 1)D torus T9,1 (which was previously found to yield the most symmetric
toroidal compactification of the superstring). We suggest how this picture might help
explain the mysterious seesaw relationship MPlMvac ≈ M2

EW between the Planck, vacuum
energy, and electroweak scales (MPl, Mvac, MEW).

Second, we explore causal set theory by replacing the traditionally random causal sets
with our ordered and highly symmetric quasi-crystalline causal sets. We provide suggestive
evidence that our spacetime quasicrystals do beat Poisson random sets in the number-
volume correspondence in both (1 + 1)D and (3 + 1)D, with the latter case conjectured to
be impossible. Finally, we attempt to understand these results by extending the concept of
hyperuniformity from space to spacetime, and we show that our (1+1)D quasicrystal is the
first structure shown to be indeed spacetime hyperuniform (we leave testing the (3 + 1)D
quasicrystal for a future work).

vi
