Defending this thesis marks not only the end of my PhD, but also my stay in Waterloo
and Perimeter (at least for now!). As a result, this is the perfect opportunity to reflect and
be grateful for all the support that I received throughout this journey.

First of all, let me take some time to properly thank my advisor, Latham Boyle, for...
everything! Literally! I do not even know where to begin, so let me start from the very
beginning. Back in 2022, Latham agreed to take me as his PhD student, but he knew he
would not stay at Perimeter for much longer (and indeed, in July 2023 he left for the Higgs
Centre at the University of Edinburgh). Somehow he managed to strike the best deal for
my interest: on the one hand, he secured funds for my PhD at Perimeter till the end (I am
grateful to Neil Turok as well for that), and on the other hand, he negotiated some more
funds on the Edinburgh side for me to visit for several months per year.

Let me pause for a second and thank the School of Physics and Astronomy and the
Higgs Center for Theoretical Physics at the University of Edinburgh for their hospitality
in the following occasions (Fall 2023, July 2024, Fall 2024, July 2025, Fall 2025 and July
2026), without which finishing this work would have been impossible. Specific thanks to
Fiona Mitchell for helping me arrange all of my visits.

Back to Latham now. Latham has such a zest for physics and mathematics, and such
broad interests and knowledge that interacting with him has been an absolute pleasure all
these years. I have learned how to make – or search for – connections between seemingly
unrelated things and I will always cherish our moments on the blackboard trying to figure
out something together. Finishing a PhD is difficult when your advisor is along the corridor,
let-alone when they are on a different continent! But we did it (almost, with the permission
of this committee), and I could not be any more grateful for knowing that Latham was
there for me when I wanted him. He introduced me to the fascinating world of aperiodic
order and together we achieved to construct the first spacetime quasicrystals.

Even though we did not end up working together, I would like to thank Niayesh Af-
shordi for being the voice-of-reason in all my PhD advisory committee meetings, for always
emphasizing that I should write my ideas1 and publish papers, which pushed me to work
harder and eventually do so.

Many thanks to my examining committee, in particular to my external examiner, Felix
Flicker, for pointing out several corrections that could me made to the thesis to improve

clarity and readability. I am also grateful for the support of my advisory committee

Next, I would like to thank my collaborators and the people that helped me with my
research all these years:

Let’s start from Part I. Working with my friends and fellow PhD students Matthew Fox

took us two more months to put our work on the arXiv from the moment we had the first
essay ready for the Gravity Research Foundation competition. I am very happy with the
final product and am looking forward to what else we can work all together.

Not all projects make it to one’s PhD thesis or to a publishable result in the strict
timeline of a PhD. This has happened to me with another project I have been working for
almost two years now with my friend and fellow PhD student Cole Coughlin (Perimeter
Institute). Cole has an infectious curiosity and enthusiasm about theoretical physics; you
can hear him talking about shapes and his voice would echo in the full Perimeter building.
We figured out so many things together when we started on a mission to reformulate the
full standard model of particle physics in terms of rotations, projections and whatnot of
polytopes in higher dimensions. I learned so many things from him already and I cannot
wait to go back to our project after this thesis is successfully submitted. A highlight in
our collaboration so far is the fact that we once made a rhombic dodecahedron from Lee
Smolin’s hangers – sorry Lee!

On that note, I would like to thank Kirill Krasnov for teaching me so many things
about spinors, the standard model and unification, and for hosting me at the University
of Nottingham. Kirill, thank you for listening to my shenanigans and for helping me think
more mathematically in order to communicate my ideas to you.

Next in the list is my former MSc-student, now PhD-brother, Alex Thorne (University
of Edinburgh). Alex was looking into a Master’s project at the intersection of quantum
error-correction, quantum gravity and quasicrystals when we first met at the TJ Walls cafe
in Edinburgh last summer. After talking to Latham, we decided to give him the project of
tiling our spacetime quasicrystals. This turned out to be a wild goose hunt, so we quickly
changed the project to studying the symmetries of spacetime quasicrystals. Alex took on
the challenge so well: not only did he come back with insightful comments on the things

I would like to thank Yasaman Yazdi (Dublin Institute for Theoretical Physics) for all

Finally, let me thank the most important person in my life, without whom completing

Chapter 1

Motivation

1.1 Is Quantum Gravity Necessary?

The road to quantum gravity is not easy. Stuck in our armchairs with little to no experi-
mental guidance, it is prudent to ponder why we think gravity is quantum-mechanical at
all. Could it be that the contrary is true, that gravity is not fundamentally quantum but
classical? Of course, this question is hardly new. It has a long and rich history, and traces
back to the seminal works of Møller [6] and Rosenfeld [7] in the 1960s.

Treating gravity classically but matter quantum-mechanically embodies semiclassical
gravity, which naturally divides into two parts. The first part is the effect of curved
spacetimes on quantum fields. This part is well-understood (full books like [8, 9, 10, 11]
have been written on it) and it has proven to be invaluable because of Hawking’s discovery
that gravitational fields can create particles [12]. The second part is the effect of quantum
fields on curved spacetimes. This part is not nearly as understood as the first, largely
because it is not clear what it means to superpose spacetimes, which appears to be an
inevitability [13].

Within the quantum gravity community, semiclassical gravity is generally regarded
as an approximation to an as yet undiscovered theory of quantum gravity [8, 9, 10, 11].
However, despite many ongoing experiments (e.g., [14, 15, 16, 17]), there is no definitive
experimental evidence that gravity is quantized. As a result, quantum gravity is supported
primarily by theoretical arguments, such as those by Eppley and Hannah [18] and Page
and Geilker [19]. However, many of these arguments are considered inconclusive [20, 21,
22, 23, 24, 25], highlighting the need for a new case for the quantization of gravity.

2



In Part I, we provide such an argument by exploring the computational consequences
of a fundamentally semiclassical world. In particular, we show that if semiclassical gravity
(as described by the semiclassical Einstein field equations) is correct, then it is possible to
solve NP-complete problems in polynomial time. As this challenges commonly held beliefs
about what is and what is not efficiently computable by physical devices (beliefs which are
encapsulated in a strong and physical version of the Church–Turing Thesis), our results
suggest that semiclassical gravity cannot be a correct description of physical reality.

Our main result hinges on an algorithm due to Bao, Bouland, and Jordan [4], which
itself is based on an earlier algorithm by Abrams and Lloyd [26]. Essentially, the Abrams–
Lloyd algorithm showed how to use Weinberg’s non-linear theory of quantum mechanics
[27] to efficiently solve hard computational problems (e.g., NP-complete problems). Several
years later, the Bao–Bouland–Jordan algorithm extended this result and showed that it is,
in fact, a more general phenomenon: basically any non-linear theory of quantum mechanics
can be used to efficiently solve hard computational problems. Our conclusions follow from
combining the Bao–Bouland–Jordan algorithm with arguments due to Bahrami et al. [24]
and Giulini et al. [28] that the weak-field evolution of a massive qubit in semiclassical
gravity is necessarily non-linear. Incidentally, our work is consistent with related work by
Kent et al. [29, 30, 31], which we discuss in Section 5.

1.2 Roaming Over the Landscape of Quantum Gravity
Theories

Having another reason to believe that gravity must be quantized, we now turn to what do
we mean by “quantum gravity”.

Over a century ago, Einstein (in fact, Minkowski) taught us that space and time are
inseparably united into a single entity: spacetime, the stage on which materials live and
evolve according to physical laws. General relativity took a bolder step further, revealing
spacetime as a dynamical stage that affects and gets affected by the materials, and whose
geometry manifests as gravity. At the same time, quantum theory showed that quantities
long assumed continuous can be fundamentally discrete. Macroscopically, materials and
spacetime appear classical, smooth and continuous. Yet, through a microscope one sees
the granularity of a slab of matter, with its atoms obeying the laws of quantum theory at
these tiny scales. The question is: “if gravity is geometry and ‘quantumness’ is discrete-
ness, would one see similar ‘geometric atoms’ if we could peak into spacetime’s
microscopic structure?”

3



There are several approaches to quantum gravity (QG) in the literature and any attempt
to provide a comprehensive review of each one of them here would be futile. For this reason,
we contain ourselves to simply mentioning some of them.

1.2.1 Discretum vs Continuum

We do so by placing them into two very broad categories: discrete and continuous theories.
Here, we focus on whether or not they describe spacetime in terms of a continuous manifold
(on which perhaps quantum fields or strings live) or replace this smooth structure with
some discrete notion of spacetime. In the discrete category, we have

• Loop Quantum Gravity (LQG) [32, 33, 34]: background-independent quantiza-
tion of Einstein’s general relativity rewritten in terms of connection variables. It has
two formulations: first, its Hamiltonian version, based on canonical quantization and
an inherent (3 + 1) splitting of spacetime. Quantizing the variables on a 3D spa-
tial slice yields the quantum states of spatial geometry, known as the spin networks.
Second, its covariant, or Lagrangian, formulation, based on the path integral. This
leads to a sum over all possible spacetime histories (geometries) in 4D, known as
spinfoams.

• Causal Dynamical Triangulations (CDTs) [35, 36, 37]: a non-perturbative lat-
tice path-integral approach that sums over all possible ways to glue flat simplicial
geometric building blocks (4-simplices, the analogues of triangles in higher dimen-
sions) together to build a triangulated spacetime.

• Causal Set Theory (CST) [38]: replaces the continuous spacetime entirely with a
discrete, partially ordered set of fundamental, indivisible spacetime elements (“events”).
The partial order explicitly represents the causal structure, meaning geometry is fun-
damentally discrete and causality is the foundational organizing principle.

Perhaps the most discrete theory out of all discrete theories is CST; this is because in the
other approaches one usually takes the limit that the discrete building blocks vanish, for
example by taking the edges of a triangulation to be zero in order to recover the continuum.

In the continuous category, we have

• String Theory (ST) [39, 40]: replaces 0D point-like particles with 1D vibrating
strings moving through a higher-dimensional spacetime, and higher-dimensional ob-
jects known as branes. Gravity emerges naturally as the lowest vibrational mode

4



of a closed string (the graviton), and the framework naturally incorporates gauge
interactions and supersymmetry.

• Asymptotic Safety (AS) [41, 42, 43, 44]: postulates that gravity remains a con-
ventional quantum field theory of metrics up to arbitrarily high energies, avoiding
standard perturbative non-renormalizability via a non-trivial, non-Gaussian ultra-
violet (UV) fixed point. Under the renormalization group flow, the gravitational
couplings are driven to finite, stable values at the Planck scale.

• Holographic Ideas [45] and AdS/CFT Correspondence [46]: postulates that
the entire informational content of a volume of space can be encoded on a lower-
dimensional boundary of that region, much like a 2D hologram contains 3D infor-
mation. Its most famous mathematical realization is the AdS/CFT correspondence,
which demonstrates a duality between a theory of quantum gravity in a bulk volume
(Anti-de Sitter space) and a non-gravitational quantum field theory defined on its
boundary (Conformal Field Theory).

A good place to look for a broad overview of all of these approaches is [47] and [48]. To this
list we shall add ideas that attempt to unify the standard model (SM) of particle physics
with gravity [49], theories based on effective field theory techniques, higher-order gravities
and more.

1.2.2 Hints of Fractality Coming from Multiple Directions

Hints of a fractal nature of spacetime pervade modern theoretical physics. Our most
successful physical theories - like the Standard Model, for example - are Quantum Field
Theories (QFTs), and any sensible QFT ‘flows’ to a conformal fixed point under the renor-
malization group either at high (UV) or low (IR) energies, where scaling symmetry becomes
important [50]. Close to their fixed points, various very distinct condensed-matter systems
share universal properties : a scale-invariant power-spectrum, characterized by a common
set of exponents. When gravity is brought within the QFT-framework, this idea is real-
ized in Asymptotic Safety [42, 44], where spacetime is continuous and this fractal scaling
symmetry is promoted to a UV-principle. Even outside of the QFT-paradigm, though, in
CDTs for instance, where spacetime is now described through a triangulation, simulations
show a dynamical dimensional reduction from 4 to 2 dimensions happening in the UV,
which can only occur for a fractal (see §7.1 in [37]).1 In the landscape of String Theory,

1Here, ‘dimension’ refers to the ‘spectral dimension’ ds ∈ R (measuring the spread of a process into
space over time; it depends on the topology of the underlying space and the diffusion rate), as opposed to

5



there is the vastly unexplored corner of quasi-crystalline orbifold compactifications, an old,
[51] but recently revisited [52] idea that spacetime can look like an orbifold with ‘forbid-
den’ symmetries. Even cosmological observations hint at an early universe characterized
by near-scale invariant power-spectrum [53], suggesting that such symmetry may be woven
into the fabric of spacetime itself.

In Part II, we take discreteness (i.e. “the quantum”) and fractality (i.e. “scaling sym-
metry”) seriously, constructing the first examples of spacetime quasicrystals with these
properties and examining their applications in different fields. These structures combine
discreteness, fractality, symmetry, and order all at once, and are a novel example of discrete
Lorentzian geometries with high degree of symmetry.

1.3 Quasicrystals and Where to Find Them

“... [The Penrose tiles] are a marvellous example of how a
mathematical discovery, made with no inkling of its appli-
cation to reality, may turn out to have been anticipated by
Mother Nature!”

1.3.1 A Journey from Space to Spacetime

Self-similar quasicrystals (like the Penrose tiling [55, 56] in Fig. 1.1) are mathematical
structures whose beautiful and unexpected properties have fascinated mathematicians since
their discovery in the 1970s [56, 57, 58, 59, 60]. Among many other fascinating features,
they: (i) are intrinsically non-periodic, yet perfectly long-range ordered (with a pure-point
diffraction spectrum, like a crystal); (ii) have a “non-crystallographic” orientational sym-
metry – too large to be compatible with any periodic pattern; for this reason, it is a
“forbidden” (for crystals) symmetry; and (iii) embody a kind of discrete scale-invariance or
self-similarity that is also impossible in a periodic pattern. Moreover, these three features

Such patterns were initially thought to be purely mathematical curiosities, but beau-
tiful mathematical structures often have a way of finding a place in the real world! In
the 1980s, these patterns turned out to be the blueprints for a new class of materials
(quasicrystals), first discovered in the lab [70], and later found to also occur naturally [71]
(forming e.g. in the birth of the Solar System [72], in lightning strikes [73], and in the first
atomic bomb test [74]). A very vivid narrative behind these discoveries is given in [75].
Since then, quasicrystals have almost entirely been studied in that context – i.e. within
condensed-matter physics, where their nature is spatial, like the materials they describe.
More recently, they have also appeared in other, completely different situations: as the

7



blueprints for quantum error correcting codes [76], and in the context of discretizing scale-
invariant/conformally-invariant systems and “discrete holography” [77, 69], all of which
suggests a possible connection to quantum gravity.

All these are examples of applications of purely spatial quasicrystals, either in Euclidean
or in hyperbolic space. Until now, nobody had succeeded in constructing analogous struc-
tures in spacetime, where causality and Lorentz symmetry are fundamental. This gap has
implicitly limited the role that aperiodic order could play in relativistic spacetime contexts
and quantum gravity.

Motivated both by these physical connections and also by pure mathematical interest, in
an earlier paper [2] we showed how self-similar quasicrystals may be naturally generalized
from Euclidean space to Minkowski spacetime. In that work, we constructed the first
examples of such Lorentzian quasicrystals, which are essentially the spacetime analogues of
Euclidean quasicrystals like the Penrose tiling or the Ammann-Beenker tiling.2 We pointed
out key novel features of these objects (compared to their Euclidean cousins), and ended
with some speculations about how such spacetime quasicrystals might relate to reality.
The present thesis is a substantial extension of this work; even though all the material
from [2] is included (and revised, to some extent) here as well, the thesis goes beyond the
original paper as mentioned in the Statement of Contributions and in the Outline.

1.4 Outline of the Thesis

This thesis contains two related – under the umbrella of quantum gravity – but highly
disproportional parts. In the first shorter part of the thesis, we give a conceptual argument
towards the necessity of quantization of gravity. The second longer part is entirely devoted
to spacetime quasicrystals, which we view as the main topic of this work. The two parts
can be read separately and could be of independent interest. The outlines may be used to
navigate through the content and contain most of the results of the two parts; they can be
found just after the beginning of each Part.

Chapter 2

A Primer on Computational
Complexity Theory

Computational complexity theory seeks to classify problems according to their intrinsic
difficulty, often by quantifying the resources (e.g., time, memory, number of pages for a
proof) required to solve them on a particular type of computer. For an introduction, see
§3 in [82]. For example, a major open question in computational complexity theory is to
lower-bound the time required to find a prime factor of a composite integer on a classical
computer. Note that, typically, the “measure” of an amount of a resource is with respect
to the number of bits it takes to encode the input.1

Even though the precise definition of a computing machine (or a computational model)
is beyond the scope of this work2, what we would like to emphasize is the intricate connec-
tion between computation and physics, most eloquently put in the following slogan form
(adapted from [26] to match the spirit of Wheeler’s saying about general relativity:

“Computation is a physical process, and the
physical laws tell us what is efficiently computable.”

This is to say, a computational model leveraging classical physics – a classical computer,
like a Python program – provides a framework that can give efficient algorithms for solving

1For example, for finding a prime factor of the number 2026, the input size is 11 (because it takes 11
bits to represent 2026 in binary ; similarly, 4 base-10 ‘digits’ in decimal), not 2026.

2We do, however, implicitly assume an abstract Turing machine, as any physical computation can be
efficiently simulated on one such device [82].

11



certain problems by manipulating the corresponding classical laws. A quantum computer,
on the other hand, has access to a different set of laws, those of quantum theory, and comes
with its own set of computational advantages and limitations. Similarly, any physical
theory can, in principle, give rise to its own computational device.

2.1 How can Computational Problems be Classified?

Given a particular resource and a type of computer, one can then discuss the class of
problems that the model can solve using an amount of the given resource. There are
several problems out there, but perhaps the most useful ones are those that are formulated
as decision problems, i.e. those whose answer is emphatically ‘YES’ or ‘NO’. This is because
other types of problems, such as search problems or counting problems (i.e. those that ask
‘which solution?’ and ‘how many solutions?’ instead of ‘does it exist any solution?’), can
usually be reduced to a series of decision problems.

Let’s see an example: consider a logical Boolean formula like

f(x1, x2, x3) = (x1 ∨ x2) ∧ (x3 ∨ ¬x2), (2.1)

where x1, x2, x3 ∈ {0, 1} are binary variables and ∨,∧ and ¬ are the logical OR, AND and
NOT operators respectively. In total, there are 23 = 8 possible truth values,

{0, 1}3 =
{
{0, 0, 0}, {1, 0, 0} (+ 3 perm.), {1, 1, 0} (+ 3 perm.), {1, 1, 1}

}
(TRUE/FALSE-assignments) for the three variables, and f evaluates to either ‘TRUE’ or
‘FALSE’ for some input x ∈ {0, 1}3. Given the expression f , Alice could ask:

“Does there exist any valid assignment to the
variables x1,2,3 that make f yield TRUE?”

This is the decision problem for f and it can be solved by brute force if, for example, one
enumerates all possible eight truth values (let’s say, by building a truth table) and check
them one by one to see if they satisfy the expression (2.1), that is, if f(x) = 1. Imagine
that one feeds f through such a decision solver and the output is f(x) = 1, so we now
know that f has a solution (i.e., that f is satisfiable). Alice’s friend, Bob, now asks:

12



“Which assignments of the variables x1,2.3 satisfies f?”

This is the search problem for f and it can be solved by a recursive procedure based on
the decision problem:

1. Pick the first (or any other) variable and set it to TRUE to obtain another expression
f(x1 = TRUE, x2, x3) = f (1).

2. Pass f (1) through the decision solver and check if it is satisfiable; if yes, lock in x1 = 1
and continue recursively to determine a satisfying assignment for f (1) with the next
variable (i.e. set x2 = TRUE to get f (2) and repeat); if no, then set x1 = 0 and
continue similarly.

3. For n Boolean variables, the process terminates after at most 2n recursive queries of
the decision solver (for non-binary variables, the number of calls becomes kn, where
k are the possible values for each variable); 2n corresponds to guessing the truth
value wrongly for each single variable xi at each iterative step of the process. The
total running time of the algorithm is

∼ (# recursive calls)× (running time it takes to solve the decision problem),

so if the decision problem can be solved relatively “quickly”, the search problem can
be too (with some manageable polynomial overhead that comes from how many times
we invoke the decision solver).

For this reason, we can focus on decision problems, which are “easier” to solve in the sense
that, if we can solve those, we can solve more problems because of that. Indeed, decision
problems are used to place problems into different computational complexity classes; some
of them are shown in Fig. 2.1 and are defined more formally in the next Section 2.2.

Let us use this example to comment on several important points which are used implic-
itly in this thesis; here, we focus on the intuition, while we refer the reader to a standard
textbook (e.g. [85]) in computational complexity theory for a formal treatment.

• Algorithmic Efficiency: when the evaluation time scales polynomially with the
input-size |x|, we say that the solution is found efficiently (or “quickly”), as opposed
to an exponential scaling, which becomes intractable very soon once |x| gets bigger
and bigger. For instance, consider two algorithms that take some input x and achieve

• Problem Reducibility: using an instance of some problem to solve another problem
is a more general phenomenon in computational complexity theory. Similar to how
the decision problem of f was used above to solve its associated search problem,
many other problems can be reduced to some alternative problems in the sense that,

14



if a solution to the latter is known or can be obtained efficiently, it can be used to
solve the original problem efficiently as well. Reductions are a very important tool, as
they offer methods to map problems of unknown complexity onto ones of known. For
example, consider a new Problem A, for which no polynomial algorithm is known;
if it can be reduced efficiently to some Problem B with a known polynomial-time
solver, this means that Problem A is at least as hard as Problem B, so they have
similar complexity and our new problem can also be solved in polynomial time. There
are several different types of reductions and their proper definitions are not entirely
relevant for us here (again, see [85]), but let us briefly mention two key ideas:

1. Karp-reductions [86] allow us to reduce Problem A to Problem B using a
polynomial-time algorithm that preserves the structural difficulty of the prob-
lem. Solving Problem A amounts to writing a function that transforms the
entire instance of Problem A into an instance of Problem B efficiently, and then
querying the solver for Problem B exactly once to get an answer to the original
question for Problem A without any further computation. Because this reduc-
tion process tell us that Problem A is at least as hard as Problem B, it is used
to define the NP-complete class (see discussion below and Fig. 2.1).

2. Oracle-reductions (or Cook/Turing-reductions) tell us if Problem A is com-
putable by Problem B no matter how complicated the latter might be. Solving
Problem A amounts to writing a function that includes a subroutine for solving
Problem B, which we are allowed to call as many times as needed. This sub-
routine is treated as a black-box “oracle”, whose inner workings are irrelevant
for solving Problem A. In fact, solving Problem B might be an exponentially
hard task, but, provided our black-box delivers a solution, the original Problem
A can be solved as well. These type of reductions are used to quantify “oracle
complexity” (how many times you need to query a black box to get an answer).

• Completeness, or the “One-Problem-to-Rule-‘Em-All” idea: reductions, in par-
ticular of the polynomial Karp-type, are very useful as they allow us to study only
certain problems that are representatives of entire complexity classes (are “complete”).
For example, a known decision problem, the Boolean satisfiability problem SAT, is
shown to be NP-complete, so any NP problem can be reduced to it “quickly” [87, 88].
Crucially, this means that all problems in NP are structurally equivalent to SAT;
finding an efficient algorithm for SAT would then imply that an efficient algorithm
exists for all NP problems (which is not expected; see next Section 2.2).3

∨ operator.4 This has been shown to be in P, but its cousin, 3-SAT, is in NP.

In this work, we are primarily concerned with how the difficulty of a problem changes
when a candidate solution, or proof, is provided. Indeed, many problems exhibit an asym-
metry in the time required to find a solution versus the time required to verify a solution.
Consider, for example, a Sudoku puzzle: checking a completed grid is far easier than con-
structing one from scratch. However, it is not known if this distinction reflects a genuine
difference in computational difficulty. In computational complexity theory, this question
is formalized in the famous P versus NP problem, which we now discuss.

2.2 The P ?
= NP Problem and the Physical Extended

Church–Turing Thesis (PECTT)

Intuitively, the complexity class P (“polynomial time”) consists of all the computational
problems that can be efficiently solved (a.k.a. decided) by a classical computer.5 For
example, deciding if a binary string is palindromic or not is in P. More formally, let
{0, 1}n be the set of all n-bit binary strings, {0, 1}∗ the set of all finite-length binary strings
(i.e., {0, 1}∗ =

⋃
n≥1{0, 1}n), and |x| the length of a string x. Then, P consists of all the

functions L : {0, 1}∗ → {0, 1} (a.k.a. languages) for which there exists a deterministic and
polynomial time classical algorithm M (i.e., a deterministic and polynomial time Turing
machine) such that for all inputs x ∈ {0, 1}∗, L(x) = 1 if and only if M(x) = 1.

On the other hand, the complexity class NP (“non-deterministic polynomial time")
consists of all of the computational problems for which a valid proof can be efficiently
checked by a classical computer. For example, the 3-SAT problem we encountered before
is in NP. In particular, L ∈ NP if and only if there exists a deterministic and polynomial
time algorithm M and a polynomial p such that for all inputs x ∈ {0, 1}∗, L(x) = 1 if and
only if there exists y ∈ {0, 1}p(|x|) (usually called a proof, certificate, or witness) such that
M(x, y) = 1. In other words, L ∈ NP if and only if for all x ∈ {0, 1}∗, if L(x) = 1, then
there exists a proof that will cause M to accept x, and if L(x) = 0, then there is no proof
that will cause M to accept x.

Evidently, P ⊆ NP, and it is a major open question (in fact, one out of the six remaining
Millennium Prize Problem [89]; the Poincaré Conjecture is now proven) whether P = NP.
Needless to say that proving this statement formally will not only earn one a substantial
amount of money, but also a great deal of fame. The general consensus, though, is that
P ̸= NP because the alternative suggests that proving a mathematical statement is just
as easy as verifying that a given proof is correct, which is something that mathematical
experience says is false [90]. A very nice review of the P vs NP problem is given in [91].

Now, the entire premise of quantum computation is that it changes the narrative of
what can and cannot be computed efficiently in the physical world. In particular, there
exist problems widely believed to be in NP\P that can be solved efficiently on a quantum
computer. The most famous such problem is integer factorization, for which Shor exhibited
his eponymous polynomial-time quantum algorithm [92].

5In fact, the set of computational problems that efficient classical computers can solve is not P, but
BPP (“bounded-error probabilistic polynomial time”), which is the probabilistic analogue of P. However,
it is generally believed that P = BPP [85], so in this discussion we have chosen to only talk about P.

That said, it is generally expected that the hardest problems in NP—the so-called
NP-complete problems—do not admit efficient quantum algorithms [82, 93]. In part, this
belief stems from the idea that NP-complete problems appear to lack the requisite struc-
ture for there to be an exponential quantum speed-up [93]. Of course, this is not to say
that quantum computers offer no advantage for these problems. Grover’s algorithm, for ex-
ample, solves any NP-complete problem quadratically faster than any classical brute-force
algorithm [94].6 However, this advantage is modest and does not provide the exponential
speed-up required to solve an NP-complete problem in polynomial time on a quantum
computer. It is also worth noting that if quantum computers cannot solve NP-complete
problems in polynomial time, then P ̸= NP [82].7

More generally, it is a tenet of quantum information theory, and of the theory of com-
putation itself, that no physically reasonable model of computation (perhaps even more
powerful than quantum computation) can efficiently solve an NP-complete problem. This
expectation is stipulated in the Physical Extended Church–Turing Thesis, which was origi-
nally proposed by Freedman, Kitaev, Larsen, and Wang in the early 2000s [96] and extended
an earlier “physical” version of the Church–Turing Thesis by Deutsch in the 1980s [97].

Physical Extended Church–Turing Thesis (PECTT). No physical procedure can de-
cide an NP-complete problem in polynomially many steps.

Let us now make a comment about the wording used above in our formulation of the
PECTT. One might wonder: “what if I get lucky and guess the solution to some given
instance of an NP-problem correctly in one step? Would that violate the PECTT?” Not so
easy, no. An NP language L corresponds to an infinite collection of problems {lx}, one for
each finite-size bit-string x. Each lx is of the form “is x in the set L”. Therefore, one might
get lucky for a few of these questions, but guessing can only take you that far, because
getting lucky for all x must have vanishingly small probability.

To close off this section, we would like to emphasize that, while motivated from com-
puter science, the PECTT is largely a postulate about the physical world as it articulates
what can and cannot be computed efficiently by physical devices. Thus, in the context
of demarcating different physical theories, the PECTT dictates that a candidate theory
should be deemed implausible if it can be exploited to efficiently solve an NP-complete
problem. Ultimately, we will show that semiclassical gravity is such a theory.

2.2.1 How Physical is the PECTT?

At first sight, it might seem that the PECTT is against the known fact that several NP-
complete and NP-hard problems can be rephrased in terms of some Ising model [98, 99], so
that they appear to be “solved” by physical systems. Usually, this is achieved by mapping a
given computationally hard problem to some Ising Hamiltonian HIsing, whose ground state
encodes information about the problem under consideration. For example, as explained
in [98], an NP-complete problem is encoded in HIsing as the decision problem “does the
ground state have energy ≤ 0?”, while an NP-hard problem becomes the optimization
problem “what is the ground state energy?”. Does this mean that the PECTT is violated
by physical systems, then, and wouldn’t this make it... unphysical?

The answer turns out to be negative. Even though there might exist a quantum system
that could solve the NP-complete or NP-hard problem, this cannot be done efficiently
on a quantum computer. Indeed, to achieve this, we would need to efficiently simulate
the quantum system, and no such process is currently known. In fact, the estimation of
the ground state of some Hamiltonian is known to be a QMA-complete problem, which is
harder than NP-complete (see [100] for appropriate definitions). As a result, even if we can
map NP problems onto physical systems, this is not enough to claim that NP is efficiently
solved on those systems.

cannot be used to argue that P = NP and thus they violate the PECTT, at least

In the context of semiclassical gravity, it has been argued that the SN dynamics together
with the instantaneous collapse prescription are inconsistent. This is because the discontin-

(∇µGµν = 0) on the left hand-side [19]. This claim has been debated in the literature
[20, 23], though, as a prescription for measurements that can be given a collapse interpre-
tation and is compatible with ∇µ⟨Ψ|T̂µνΨ⟩ = 0 has been worked out in [8] (but it restricts
the possible Ψ states that satisfy it).

On the other hand, the SN dynamics are a deterministic non-linear quantum evolution
equation, and as such, they also suffer from superluminal signalling [120, 121, 122]. This
issue also holds for Weinberg’s non-linear quantum theory [27], the one that the original
Abrams–Lloyd paper wanted to rule out [26]. Yet, a more careful relativistic treatment of
quantum states suggests that non-linearities can exist without necessarily leading to super-
luminal communication with localized collapse [29]. As a result, (weak-field) semiclassical
gravity in the spirit of the SN equation could still be made consistent, and a framework
that employs it is the quantum readout devices of [30] – we’ll come back to it in the next
Chapter. The point is that, if SN dynamics are not unequivocally ruled out by some other
condition, they imply efficient solutions to NP-complete problems, which contradicts the
PECTT.

Indeed, non-linearities, faster-than-light communication and vast computational ad-
vantages are very much related, as was established in the original Bao–Bouland–Jordan
paper [4]. There, the authors point out that “the no-signalling principle is equivalent to the

inability to solve NP-hard problems efficiently by brute force within the classes of theories
analyzed” (their wording), and generic non-linearities (that satisfy Theorem 2) are included
in those theories. It would be interesting to investigate whether these results can be ex-

in the objective collapse models. If so, one could appeal to the no-signalling condition to
argue that they are unphysical, and thus the PECTT survives. In the authors’ own words,

“Thus, the quantum Church–Turing thesis appears to be remarkably robust,
depending not in a sensitive way on the complete Hilbert-space formalism of
quantum mechanics, but rather derivable from more foundational operational
principles such as the impossibility of superluminal signalling.”

Chapter 5

Discussion: Gravity from the Lens of
Computational Complexity Theory

In Part I, we showed that the weak-field dynamics of the semiclassical EFEs can efficiently
solve NP-complete problems. In consequence, if gravity is fundamentally classical and if
the semiclassical EFEs describe the matter-gravity coupling, then one can efficiently solve
NP-complete problems.

As this violates the PECTT, we are led to the conclusion that gravity is not classical. Of
course, there are many ways that one may try to evade this conclusion. Another scenario,
for example, is that gravity is classical, but the semiclassical EFEs do not correctly describe
the matter-gravity coupling. Alternatively, one could simply reject the PECTT altogether.
Yet each such move comes at a conceptual cost and requires considerable justification.

5.1 Scenario 1: Gravity is Classical with a Different
Gravity–Matter Coupling

To avoid quantizing gravity, then, perhaps we can keep gravity classical but modify the
non-linear structure of the matter-gravity coupling.

However, given the incredibly general nature of Theorem 2, our results suggest that,
in fact, any consistent, semiclassical, and non-linear matter-gravity coupling will entail
an efficient algorithm to solve NP-complete problems and thus violate the PECTT. We
therefore take our results not as an argument for an alternative theory of semiclassical
gravity, but rather as an argument for the quantization of gravity itself.

32



What about a linear coupling then? Could that lead to a consistent semiclassical
theory? Here, there is the example of Oppenheim’s post-quantum theory of classical gravity
[123], where the dynamics are such that the density matrix of a quantum state evolves
linearly and stochastically. Similar to the objective collapse models, the stochasticity of
the dynamics evades our current argument from Chapter 4. Hence, our conclusions do
not hold, and there is no obvious violation of the PECTT for this theory1. However, as is
argued in [23] (their wording):

“Rather than a single spacetime manifold, these models describe statistical en-
sembles of spacetimes. Therefore, strictly speaking, they do not qualify as mod-
els of semiclassical gravity as defined here2, but could potentially be regarded as
a theory of (semi-)classical statistical mechanics for such models.“

In other words, this linear and stochastic theory already goes beyond traditional semiclas-
sical gravity – in a sense, it is more towards the quantum side of gravity already, so more
within the realm of quantum gravity rather than semiclassical gravity.

5.2 Scenario 2: the PECTT is Violated

What if we just ignore the PECTT? This would mean that we believe that efficient solutions
to NP-complete problems are, in principle, attainable by some physical machine operating
under the laws of a physical theory. We choose not to comment here on the possible
sci-fi scenarios arising in a world where P = NP, such as the breaking of encryption and
the collapse of digital privacy, or the possibility of machines “taking over mathematics”
and automatically generate formal proofs for mathematical conjectures or simulating our
hardest known computational problems3. Instead, we would like to answer “why do we
believe in the PECTT?” and what does this entail.

1 It is worth mentioning that, according to a more general analysis given in [124], any consistent
(definition made precise in the paper) coupling between classical gravity and quantum matter must be
fundamentally irreversible. This analysis is based on General Probabilistic Theories (GPTs), a framework
that includes quantum theory but goes beyond that. This result is consistent with Oppenheim’s theory, but
not with the weak-field limit of the semiclassical EFEs, as those are reversible (the SN map is invertible).

2For semiclassical gravity, they assume a classical spacetime, i.e. a pseudo-Riemannian 4-manifold
(M, g) with metric gµν , not a superposition thereof.

3Some might argue that the latter scenario is currently unfolding; yet, as far as P ̸= NP, traditional –
“human” – mathematics could still be safe from the “machines”.

33



First, let us rephrase the PECTT in plainer language: it states that “whatever the
correct physical description of the world is, and whatever complexity class C of efficiently
computable languages it gives rise to, NP is not in C”. Second, let us wonder: what could be
this physical theory? As far as we know, our best contender for C at the moment is BQP,
which can be thought of as the set of decision problems solvable on a quantum circuit with
polynomially many gates [85]. The PECTT, then, postulates that NP ̸⊂ BQP, which is a
commonly held conjecture usually referred to as the quantum Church–Turing Thesis ; this
is the statement put forward first by Deutsch [97] and then by Freedman, Kitaev, Larsen,
and Wang [96]. As we mentioned in Footnote 6 in Chapter 2.2, proving the conjecture
would be a proof of P ̸= NP too. And how robust is BQP as a candidate for C? In the
words of Bao, Bouland and Jordan [4], very:

Physical processes which conceivably might be more computationally powerful
than quantum Turing machines, such as various quantum many-body dynamics
of fermions, bosons, and anyons, as well as scattering processes in relativis-
tic quantum field theories, can all be simulated with polynomial overhead by
quantum circuits”, see [96, 125, 126, 127, 128]

We shall mention one more result in support of the claim that physical theories cannot
compute NP efficiently. First, a framework that generalizes that of quantum theory is
provided by the GPTs (see Footnote 1). Now, in [129], it is shown that the set of problems
that a GPT can solve is BGP (the general-probabilistic analogue of BQP; it holds that
BQP ⊆ BGP) does not include NP.4 Even in the presence of gravity, if any consistent
gravity-matter coupling (assuming the former is classical) is described by some GPT (with
an irreversible interaction) as argued in [124], this tells us that the theory cannot efficiently
compute NP either. Additionally, if the gravitational field is non-classical (and thus with
a reversible interaction) and still describable in terms of a GPT, this theory of “quantum
gravity” would still not be able to compute NP in polynomial time.

In this work, we do not say that BQP is necessarily the abstract complexity class C,
though there is good evidence that it might be. We do say, though, that when one brings
in semiclassical gravity in our physical description, C becomes so big that it includes NP.
This goes against our PECTT conjecture, which tells us that efficient computation of
NP-languages is unphysical.5

4They also show in [129] that, even allowing for post-selection (i.e. the imaginary ability to keep only the
successful runs of a computation and throw away all other runs), PostBGP ⊆ PostBQP, and post-selection
is known to give rise to extremely powerful quantum computers [130]. Consequently, even post-selected
general-probabilistic computers are not more powerful than post-selected quantum computers.

5See also [131] for the computational power of physical operational theories. The PECTT conjecture

34



While preparing this manuscript, we became aware of the series of works [29, 30, 31]
by Kent et al. concerning hypothetical “readout devices” capable of extracting classical
information from a quantum system without disturbing it. In [30], it was argued that
semiclassical gravity may provide a physically realizable readout mechanism and, more-
over, that such devices could in principle implement the original Abrams–Lloyd algorithm
in [26] for solving NP-complete problems. In this respect, their framework is closely re-
lated to the gravitational mechanism studied here, but our conclusions differ primarily in
their interpretation. Specifically, whereas Kent et al. emphasize the possibility that such
dynamics could lead to experimentally accessible computational advantages beyond stan-
dard quantum theory, we emphasize that there is a profound tension between such vast
computational consequences and the PECTT. Thus, insofar as one regards the PECTT as
a fundamental principle of physics, such readout devices cannot exist.

5.3 Scenario 3: Gravity is not Classical

Finally, let us argue briefly that, in a world without unphysical exponential speed-ups and
ad-hoc gravity-matter couplings6, quantizing gravity might be the simplest way to respect
the PECTT.

The reason is that quantizing gravity restores linearity and thus avoids our argument
altogether. For example, in the specific context of the weak-field limit of the semiclassical
EFEs, quantizing the spacetime metric causes the self-gravitational potential in the SN
equation to drop out, thus linearizing the dynamics [132, 28].7 Consequently, at least in
this case, our argument in Section 4.2 does not apply, and the PECTT is not obviously
violated. It would be interesting to see whether our existing quantum gravity frameworks
predict linear or non-linear evolutions for the quantum state.

Ultimately, we hope our results inspire a more computational way of thinking about
demarcating fundamental physical theories. While gravitational physics and computational
complexity theory are rather disparate fields, here we have demonstrated an intriguing
consistency check between the two. Specifically, if the PECTT is taken seriously as a

PECTT, and computational complexity more broadly, provides not just a constraint, but
a guiding principle in the search for a consistent theory of quantum gravity.

dimensional lattice, and projecting nearby lattice points onto the cut) in Section 7.1, we de-

choose lattice points near the cut, we also discuss a more general CNP scheme based on a
“weighting function”, which weights different points differently, according to their distance
from the cut. This allows us to define “self-dual” and “globally-scale-invariant” quasicrys-
tals, which will be important when we turn to Lorentzian quasicrystals. To illustrate all of

While Chapter 7 is mainly a review, the reader may find certain aspects of our for-
mulation novel or helpful, as it has been designed (i) to clarify the logical connection
between quasi-periodicity, non-crystallographic symmetry and discrete self-similarity or
scale-invariance; and (ii) relatedly, to make the generalization from Euclidean to Lorentzian
spacetime simple and natural (and, to our knowledge, our notions of self-dual and globally-
scale-invariant quasicrystals are also new.)

If we draw all the mirrors in a given reflection group G, they divide up the space Yk into
a set of congruent convex fundamental domains, which together form a tessellation T
of Yk. We also say that G tiles Yk by reflections. If we pick one such fundamental domain
(or Coxeter polytope) Γ, the fundamental roots are the outward pointing normal vectors
to its bounding mirror “faces” (or the hyperplanes defining them). So the corresponding
Coxeter diagram specifies the shape of the fundamental domain Γ: the number of its faces,
and the angle at which each pair of faces meets (see Fig. 6.2). The symmetries of the
Coxeter diagram reflect symmetries of the Coxeter polytope itself: e.g. the Z2 symmetry
of the An, Dn and E6 graphs, or the larger S3 symmetry of the D4 graph which gives rise
to the famous triality symmetry of the so(8) Lie algebra (see Section 6.3 and Appendix
B for triality). Given a choice of fundamental domain Γ, successive reflections through its
faces can map it to any other copy of Γ in the tessellation T of Yk, so that the “tiles” in T
are in one-to-one correspondence with the elements in the group G.

The spherical Coxeter groups have been completely classified (see the left panel
of Fig. 6.1), and, moreover, Coxeter showed that these are precisely the finite Coxeter

groups. They capture symmetries of regular polytopes in flat Euclidean space [138] and
their finiteness manifests itself in the fact that the sphere they tessellate by reflections is
chopped into a finite number of tiles, each of finite volume (see Fig. 6.2).

To get some intuition about them, we introduce at this point the Schläfli symbol,
a shorthand for representing regular polytopes or regular tessellations by polytopes: {p}
denotes a (convex) regular p-gon in 2-dimensional space;5 {3}, {4} and {6}, for example,

6.2.2 Crystallographic vs Non-Crystallographic Coxeter Groups

Another very important distinction of Coxeter groups, in particular in terms of the theory
of lattices and quasicrystals, is the following. A Coxeter group is crystallographic if
its geometric representation in V = Rn (the space spanned by the n fundamental roots)
can stabilize a lattice Λ in V (i.e. the Z-span of some basis of V ). Otherwise it is non-
crystallographic. A necessary and sufficient condition for a Coxeter group to be crys-
tallographic is that: (i) all of the edges in its Coxeter diagram are labelled by 2, 3, 4, 6,
or ∞; and (ii) for each circuit (closed loop) in the Coxeter diagram, the number of edges
labelled 4 (resp. 6) around the circuit is even (see Sec. 6.6 in [65]). When either (i) or (ii)
is not met, the group is non-crystallographic; in the remainder of this work, we take this
to be the definition of a non-crystallographic group.

At this point, it will be useful to introduce two different concepts of the “rank” of a
Coxeter group; definitions are from [5]. So far, we have been referring to the ordinary
rank of a Coxeter group G as the number of its fundamental roots. Equivalently, this is
also the dimension of the vector space V (over R) on which G has a geometric (reflection)
representation. Using the definitions of the previous paragraph, we can write that V =
Λroot ⊗ R = spanR{ri}i=1,...,n = Rn. As a result, the ordinary rank n of G, then, is the
dimension of the real vector space V generated by taking all real linear combinations of
roots of G (over R, Λroot and Λall roots are obviously the same sets, equal to the the full V ).
Over Q, though, things change: we refer to the rational rank nQ of G as the dimension
of the vector space (over Q) generated by all rational linear combinations of roots. We
write VQ = Λall roots ⊗ Q = QnQ . When G is crystallographic, n = nQ always; in the non-
crystallographic case, nQ > n always. For the example of I52 we just saw, the ordinary
rank is n = 2, but its rational rank is nQ = 4, as it takes two rational numbers to express
the golden ratio ϕ. Thus, as mentioned poetically in [5], “a non-crystallographic Coxeter
group lives a double life: in one sense, its roots live in the lower-dimensional space Rn; but
in another sense, they live in the higher-dimensional space QnQ .”

Remarkably, we can make a different structure that does have one of the forbidden (for
lattices) non-crystallographic symmetries at the cost of losing translational symmetry (i.e.
periodicity). These non-crystallographic groups play an important role in the theory of
quasi-periodic tilings and quasicrystals [59], where they govern the orientational symmetries
of such structures: e.g. the 2D Penrose tiling (with decagonal orientational symmetry I102 )
[55, 168], the 2D Ammann-Beenker tiling (with octagonal symmetry I82 ) [169, 170], various
3D quasicrystals and tilings (with icosahedral symmetry H3) [59], and the 4D Elser-Sloane
quasicrystal (with symmetry H4) [171]. We will see several examples of quasicrystals and
their symmetries in the next chapters of this thesis.

6.2.3 The Spherical Coxeter Pairs through Folding

As we will see shortly in Chapter 7, quasicrystals can ultimately be obtained from appro-
priate lattices by a delicate projection method in which they inherit the lattice’s order but
not their periodicity. Their non-crystallographic symmetry, which by itself cannot exist in
any periodic pattern, turns out to be a subgroup of a crystallographic group that stabilizes
a perfectly periodic lattice in higher dimensions. This is an example of a Coxeter pair:
a pairing of two Coxeter groups out of which the parent group is higher-dimensional and
crystallographic, while the daughter group is lower-dimensional and non-crystallographic.

For the spherical Coxeter groups, all the possible Coxeter pairs have been identified in
[5]. The most interesting cases are the fivefold symmetric ones related to the golden ratio

6.3 Symmetries of Lattices

Given a lattice Λ in a vector space V , we can define two notions of symmetry transforma-
tions for Λ. First, thinking of Λ as just the underlying Z-module that it is according to the
definition (6.1), we consider the group of linear (invertible) transformations from V → V
that map Λ to itself,

GL(Λ) = {M ∈ GL(V ) |MΛ = Λ} . (6.24)

These are the automorphisms of Λ as a Z-module. After choosing a basis for Λ, this
group is isomorphic to GL(d,Z) (see discussion about bases below Eq. (6.1)). Its elements
preserve the lattice but need not preserve the Euclidean or Lorentzian metric that V might
be equipped with.

Now, if we also consider the inner product ⟨ , ⟩ on V and we ask which transformations in
GL(V ) also preserve the inner product between vectors, we arrive at the second symmetry
group. We call this the automorphism group of Λ (thought of as a Z-module that also
lives in a space with a metric), and we denote it as Aut(Λ). In other words,

Aut(Λ) = GL(V ) ∩O(V ). (6.25)

and Aut(Λ) is a discrete subgroup of the orthogonal group O(V ). The reason why we give
the name Aut(Λ) to this second group rather than the first one is because the Coxeter
group lives within Aut(Λ), as reflections ‘care’ about the metric too (as can be understood
by looking at the definition of reflections (6.12)).

A root of the lattice Λ is a vector r of positive norm N(r) = ⟨r, r⟩ > 0 for which the
associated reflection is a symmetry of Λ. If Λ is self-dual, its roots are just the lattice
vectors r ∈ Λ whose norm N(r) equals 1 or 2. In particular, the lattice vectors with
N(r) = 1 or N(r) = 2 are called the short roots and long roots, respectively [61].

The group generated by reflections in the mirrors corresponding to these roots is the
reflection subgroup ΓΛ of Aut(Λ), a Coxeter group. An important subclass of lattices are

63



reflective lattices – these are lattices for which the reflection subgroup ΓΛ has finite index
in Aut(Λ) [148, 179]. In other words, in a reflective lattice, nearly all of the automorphisms
are generated by reflections in mirrors. In these cases, we let15

Aut(Λ) = ΓΛ ⋊ Sym(Γ), (6.26)

where Sym(Γ) describe the symmetries of the fundamental convex polyhedron for the
lattice Λ, the Coxeter polytope. Geometrically, ΓΛ maps each Coxeter polyhedron Γ to one
another, whereas Sym(Γ) fixes a polyhedron and describes its symmetries, or equivalently,
the symmetries of the Coxeter-Dynkin graph of ΓΛ (see Fig. 6.2). The index of the reflection
group inside Aut(Λ) is denoted by [Aut(Λ) : ΓΛ], and by Lagrange’s theorem (the orbit-
stabilizer theorem) [180], it is equal to the order of the group Sym(Γ), |Sym(Γ)|. If Γ has
finite volume, the number of its geometric symmetries must be finite, meaning the index is
finite. This is an alternative definition for reflective lattices, as those whose fundamental
polyhedra have finite volume16.

Quasicrystals in Euclidean Space

Quasicrystals are aperiodic patterns that nevertheless have a pure-point Fourier trans-
form (diffraction pattern), like a periodic crystal [187]. For particularly interesting qua-
sicrystals like the Penrose tiling or Ammann-Beenker tiling, these properties (along with a
type of discrete scale invariance or self-similarity) follow from the quasicrystal’s underlying
orientational symmetry.

In this section we introduce the cut-and-project (CNP) scheme for constructing qua-
sicrystals – first the ordinary CNP scheme in Sec. 7.1, and then the symmetric CNP (sCNP)
scheme in Sec. 7.2 – before discussing the symmetries of these quasicrystals in Sec. 7.3.
First, let us introduce some terminology: given a d-dimensional lattice Λ ∈ Rd, and a
k-dimensional subspace W ⊂ V , we say that W is:

• rational if W ∩ Λ has rank r = k.

• partially irrational if W ∩ Λ has rank 0 < r < k,

• totally irrational if W ∩ Λ has rank 0.

In other words, the subspace W is totally irrational if it intersects the origin of Λ, but no
other points in Λ.

are also referred to as model sets in the mathematical literature [59] (see their §7).

7.2 The Symmetric CNP (sCNP) Scheme

In the general CNP scheme of Section 7.1, a particular quasicrystal is specified by mak-
ing three choices. But the most interesting quasicrystals (e.g. the Penrose tiling or the
Ammann-Beenker tiling) are produced by a more refined version of this scheme, which we
will call the “symmetric cut-and-project” (or sCNP scheme).

7.2.1 Construction

In the sCNP scheme, we again make three choices:

• Choice 1: a d-dimensional lattice Λt in V = Rd with automorphism group Aut(Λ).

• Choice 2: a non-crystallographic subgroup G ⊂ Aut(Λ), and a decomposition V =
Vph ⊕ Vin that is invariant under G: Πph = gΠphg

−1 (or equivalently [Πph, g] = 0),
∀g ∈ G.

• Choice 3: a window W ⊂ Vin or weighting function W : Vin → C invariant under
G: i.e. W = gW or W (vin) = W (g vin), ∀g ∈ G.

This produces a quasicrystal with orientational symmetry G (in the sense discussed below,
Sec. 7.3). Note that the total irrationality of Vph and Vin now follows from the fact that G
is non-crystallographic.

not construct explicitly here) are not tilings in the usual sense.

7.3.5 Local Scale Invariance

Informally, local scale invariance (also known as local inflation/deflation symmetry – LIDS
[59]) refers to the inflation/deflation phenomenon exhibited by self-similar aperiodic tilings
like the Penrose tiling or Ammann-Beenker (AB) tiling. Using the AB tiling for illustration,
we define an inflation rule, where we cut each large (purple) rhombus or square into a
certain fixed pattern of smaller (pink) rhombi and squares, as shown in Fig. 7.4.5 By
cutting up all the tiles of any AB tiling (the “parent” AB tiling) in this way and rescaling
it by the “silver ratio” 1+

√
2, we obtain another legal AB tiling (the “offspring” AB tiling).

This inflation process may be iterated arbitrarily many times.

We can also consider the inverse process, deflation, in which we glue the tiles of an
offspring AB tiling into “supertiles,” again according to the pattern in Fig. 7.4, to recover
the parent AB tiling from which it descended. In a legal AB tiling, there is a unique
way to group all the tiles into supertiles in this way, so one can unambiguously determine
the parent AB tiling from its offspring, and this deflation process may also be iterated
indefinitely.

To introduce local scale invariance more abstractly, we first review another idea: local
equivalence.

• Local equivalence. Two patterns P and P ′ (which could be tilings, quasicrystals

(where λP ′ means the pattern P ′, expanded by the factor λ). The pattern λP ′ is

and the local rule for obtaining P from P ′ is the corresponding deflation rule.

For example (see Fig. 7.4): the Ammann-Beenker tiling (in purple) is not only locally
equivalent to its inflation (in pink), it is also locally indistinguishable from its inflation
(after rescaling the pink tiling by the appropriate scale factor, 1+

8.2 Spacetime CNP Scheme

In the previous section, we first introduced the ordinary cut-and-project (CNP) scheme,
followed by the more refined Symmetric CNP scheme, in which quasi-periodicity, orienta-
tional symmetry and discrete scale symmetry (inflation/deflation symmetry) are tightly
interconnected. The most interesting quasicrystals are produced by the sCNP scheme. As
discussed in Sec. 7.2, an sCNP quasicrystal is determined by three choices, so in this section
we review these three choices (in blue boxes), and discuss any novelties associated with
generalizing each one to the Lorentzian spacetime context.

8.2.1 The Lattice Λ

Choice 1: a d-dimensional lattice Λt in V = Rd with automorphism group Aut(Λ).

Now Λ is a Lorentzian lattice in V = Rs,1. Whereas Aut(Λ) for a Euclidean lattice was
a finite group, Aut(Λ) for a Lorentzian lattice in dimension s + 1 ≥ 3 can be an infinite
group: in particular,

1. for an odd or even self-dual lattice Is,1 and IIs,1 (see Figs. 8.1a and 8.1b);

2. for any Lorentzian root lattices, i.e. the integer span of the fundamental roots of
any of the crystallographic hyperbolic Coxeter groups enumerated in Secs. 6.7–6.9
and Figs. 2 & 3 of Ref. [65].

In this Chapter, we will mostly focus on the self-dual lattices; after all, the nicest quasicrys-
tals in Euclidean space are constructed from either a hypercubic or the E8 lattice, which
are themselves self-dual. In Chapter 9 we will tackle more general Lorentzian lattices.

8.2.3 The Window

Choice 3: a window W ⊂ Vin or weighting function W : Vin → C invariant under

In the Euclidean case, since the non-crystallographic group G was a finite group, the
window W ∈ Vin or weighting function W : Vin → C only needed to have finite/discrete
rotational symmetry. For example, the 8-fold symmetric Ammann-Beenker tiling was
produced by an 8-fold symmetric window W (see Fig. 7.3).

By contrast, in the Lorentzian case, since the non-crystallographic group G has infinite
order, a symmetric window W or weighting function must also have a infinite rotational
symmetry. Since the group I∞2 (λ+0 ) exists within all (bicolourable, otherwise just take its
subgroup generated by a Coxeter element) hyperbolic Coxeter groups and it acts as an
irrational rotation on each of the Coxeter planes within the internal space, our window W
must be a polytope with a countably infinite number of edges. This is a polytope known as
an apeirogon [138]. A regular apeirogon can be defined as a partition of the Euclidean line
E1 into infinitely many equal-length segments.4 Going back to our discussion in Section
8.1.3, we can now see that this is indeed the case for the boost-plane V0: under the action
of C, E1 splits into segments of length F0. We can see that on the left of Fig. 8.2.

The situation on the internal Coxeter planes is a bit more interesting, as we can see
on the right hand-side of Fig. 8.2. The irrational Coxeter rotation chops the circle S1 into
different overlapping segments of arch-length Fj. Connecting successive points under this
rotation, one gets a star apeirogon or apeirogram [196]. A star polygon (or stellated
polygon) is a geometric shape created by extending the edges of a convex regular polygon
outwards until they intersect to form a new, star-like closed – but non-convex – boundary.
This process, known as stellation, produces self-intersecting shapes. One can think, for
example, of the regular pentagon as the shape we get by connecting each vertex by an edge
to another vertex which is 2π/5 away on S1. This way we get a partition of S1 onto 5 equal-
length fundamental domains, which are permuted by a rational rotation (by 2π/5). On
the other hand, if one connects each vertex to another vertex which is now 4π/5 away, we
get a regular star pentagon, or pentagram; for this shape, it looks as if the 5 fundamental
domains are each 4π/5 wide and overlap one another. While all such star polygons have a
finite number of vertices, edges and winding number (i.e. the number of rotations needed
to close the star), an irrational rotation produces a failed star polygon, which has infinitely

8.3 Other implications

Let us mention some other novel features of Lorentzian quasicrystals (compared to their
Euclidean cousins).

8.3.1 Point Set, But No Tiling

So far have described the sCNP algorithm with symmetric window W as a way to generate
a G-symmetric quasi-crystalline point set (for some non-crystallographic group G). But in
the Euclidean case (where G is a finite group), one can often (as in the Penrose tiling, or

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-gap_theorem


Ammann-Beenker tiling) regard these points as the endpoints of edges; these edges as the
boundaries of faces, etc, so that the G-symmetric point-set is promoted to a G-symmetric
tiling or tessellation (see Section 7.2.4).

By contrast, in the Lorentzian case, one cannot promote aG-symmetric Lorentzian sCNP
point set to a G-symmetric tiling (with a finite number of polygonal tiles). As mentioned
in Section 7.2.4, if the G-symmetric tiling contains any tile T , it must also contain the
“rotated” tile gT (∀g ∈ G). But if G is an infinite group, this will either imply that the tile
T is accompanied by an infinite number of other, differently-oriented tiles, or else, T must
be invariant under a finite-index subgroup of G (in which case the tile itself is “spherically
symmetric”). We summarize this result in the following no-go theorem:

No-Tile Theorem. One cannot promote a G-invariant spacetime quasicrystal to a G-
invariant spacetime quasi-tiling with a finite number of polygonal tiles for any infinite
non-crystallographic symmetry group G.

In fact, having an infinite number of tiles might not be too restricting at all. For
example, the pinwheel tilings [197, 198, 199] (see also §6.6 in [59]) have also an infinite
number of tiles; the simplest such tiling has infinitely many rotated copies of a single
triangular tile, all congruent to the original. Thus, there is only a single equivalence class
of tiles, but it contains infinitely many members. Such tilings, though, lack a property that
the rest of the tilings we considered so far had: they do not have finite local complexity
(FLC). Loosely speaking, tilings with FLC have their prototiles arranged only in a finite
number of possible configurations (or types of adjacencies). More formally, we say that a
pattern P ⊂ V has FLC (with respect to translations) if, for every compact region K ⊂ V ,
the collection of K and all its translated copies, {(t+K) ∩ P | t ∈ V }, contains only a
finite number of configurations of fragments inside it [59]. The pinwheel tilings do not have
FLC according to this definition. However, one can define FLC more generally with respect
to the full group of isometries of V , Iso(V ); this includes translations and rotations, if V is
Euclidean (these are also called Euclidean motions), and the full Poincaré transformations
(the latter + Lorentz boosts), if V is Lorentzian. Then, the pinwheel tiling considered in
§6.6 of [59] has FLC with respect to Euclidean motions, which explains its high degree of
order over long scales.

The pinwheel tilings are part of a family of structures with infinite local complexity
(ILC) instead – with respect to translations – and their theory has been understood to
some extent in the works of [200, 201, 202] (see references therein). More strictly, then,
what we have shown above in our No-Tile Theorem is not that we cannot tile our spacetime
quasicrystals at all, but even if we could, they would have ILC instead of FLC.7 Having said

7We thank our external examiner, Felix Flicker, for pointing out this possibility to us during the defence.

100



that, it would be interesting to explore whether it is still possible to have a G-invariant
spacetime quasi-tiling with a finite number of equivalence classes of tiles, each of them
having infinitely many members related by the infinite symmetry group.

If such a G-symmetric spacetime quasi-tiling exists, then, could it still be obtained
via sCNP? That we do not know. The reason is that the pinwheel tilings are not known
to arise via the CNP method because of their dense, circular rotational symmetry (similar
to our spacetime quasicrystals, their rotational symmetry is generated by some irrational
rotation). Instead, they are usually defined in terms of substitution rules (inflation and
subdivision of tiles). Within the sCNP framework, we can understand why we cannot tile our
spacetime quasicrystals with the traditional methods as follows: the circular (or poly-disk)
window W is simply too smooth (with “infinite edges”) to lift to some higher-dimensional
cell FΛ ∈ V with a finite number of faces that can give the lower-dimensional tiles (see
Section 7.2.4). To define the tiling with the inflate-subdivide-inflate prescription used in
the pinwheel tiling, on the other hand, we would need to know at least some prototiles,
which we do not know either. We are led to conclude, then, that if such a tiling exists, it
would demand new methods for its construction.

Finally, it is also worth mentioning that traditional metric-based approaches that tes-
sellate Euclidean point sets – such as Voronoi’s tessellation algorithm, or its dual, Delone’s8

triangulation algorithm (see §2.2 in [59] and [61])– would not work in our case. This is
because of the indefiniteness of the Minkowski metric, which allows both spacelike and
timelike distances.9 On a spacetime quasi-crystalline pattern, this issue manifests in an
inherent non-locality : for example, for any given point, its nearest neighbour (the point
closest to being spacetime-distance zero away from it) might lie very far away from it on
the pattern. We will come back to this in Section 12.5.

uniquely lifts to a cell FΛ ∈ V whose vertices have rational coordinates in the lattice basis,

Is there a natural size for the spherically-symmetric window W in the Lorentzian case?
The answer appears to be negative: the larger the radius, the denser the projected set

8.3.3 No Local Scale Invariance

In Section 7.3.4, we explained two notions of scale invariance: local and global. And, in
particular, in 7.3.5 we explained that a CNP quasicrystal has local scale invariance – also
known as “local inflation/deflation symmetry” (LIDS) – if and only if the inflated window
W̃ can be obtained via a finite number of unions and intersections of translated copies
of the original window W ; and vice versa [192, 59]. For a spherically-symmetric window
this is impossible (a rescaled ball cannot be expressed as a finite number of unions and
intersections of translated copies of the original ball). So a G-symmetric spacetime qua-
sicrystal (with infinite non-crystallographic symmetry group G) cannot have local inflation
invariance.

8.3.4 Self-Duality and Global Scale-Invariance

So far in Sec. 8.3 we have focused on spacetime sCNP quasicrystals produced via the window
scheme; and we have seen that (in the spacetime context) there is no G-invariant tiling
associated with the resulting quasi-crystalline point set, no preferred size of the window W
(and hence no preferred density of the point set), and no local inflation-deflation symmetry.

Let us turn to consider spacetime sCNP quasicrystals produced via the weighting scheme:

• If we take the weighting function W to be a Gaussian, there is a preferred width
of the Gaussian – namely the width that makes the quasicrystal self-dual, just as
explained in Sec. 7.1.3.

• If we take the weighting function W to be a power law, we obtain a quasicrystal with
global scale invariance, just as explained in Sec. 7.3.6.

102



• In particular, if we take the particular case of a trivial power law, W (vin) = 1, so
we project each point in the lattice Λ with equal weight, we effectively obtain the
dense point set Λph = ΠphΛ. This does indeed have global scale invariance: when
this dense set is rescaled by certain special numbers, it is precisely mapped to itself,
one-to-one. These special numbers are the real units of the algebraic number field
associated with the eigenvalues of the Coxeter element (see Appendix A.3)

Given all of these observations, we see that in the spacetime context, the weighting scheme
is more natural than the window scheme; and the self-dual or globally-scale-invariant qua-
sicrystals produced by the weighting scheme are most natural of all.
