Chapter 9

Generalized Spacetime CNP Scheme

In Chapter 8, we chose a particular non-crystallographic symmetry group – the one gen-
erated by the Coxeter element – and very specific lattices – the integer self-dual ones
– in order to produce the first examples of spacetime quasicrystals. Under the current
spacetime sCNP construction of Section 8.2, all dph-dimensional spacetime quasicrystals
transform under a discrete subgroup of

SO(1, 1)× SO(2)× · · · × SO(2)︸ ︷︷ ︸
(dph−2)/2 factors

which is dense in the rotational part, so spacetime quasicrystals have dramatically more
orientational symmetry than their Euclidean counterparts. However, there are several
somewhat unsatisfying and deeply interrelated facts about such constructed spacetime
quasicrystals:

• The Curse of Being Even: they can only have even dimension; to go to odd-
dimensional structures while keeping the symmetric Coxeter planes intact (i.e. re-
specting the pairing of the Coxeter eigenbasis), one would need to include the ratio-
nal direction (eigenvector v2k+1, see Section 8.1.3) to the physical space Vph, but this
would make Vph only a partially irrational subspace (see beginning of Chapter 7).

• The Only Building Block is 2: the symmetry group generated by the Coxeter
element, or the bigger infinite dihedral group (8.8), only possess 2-dimensional ir-
reducible representations 2. Any higher-dimensional quasicrystal, like the (3 + 1)D
examples of Section 8.4, does not transform in a irreducible 4 representation but in
a direct sum of appropriate numbers of 2’s (see Eq. (8.6)).

111



• Preferred Spacetime Splitting: as a result, there is always a preferred splitting
of spacetime into two-dimensional Coxeter planes, which are crucially not mixed
by the symmetry group. There is the Lorentzian V0 plane where one can boost
(and there is an infinite set of discrete boosts that are symmetries of the pattern),
and (dph − 2)/2 Euclidean planes where one could rotate (and one could practically
do any planar rotation), but one cannot mix and match. Physically, one cannot mix
the time direction hiding inside V0 with any of the spatial directions that are not
inside V0, and one could not similarly rotate two spatial directions of one Euclidean
plane into those of another such plane.

In short, the symmetry group of a spacetime quasicrystal is not a subgroup of SO(1, dph−1).
Therefore, a question arises naturally: can we do better? Can we make our spacetime
quasicrystals have even more intricate symmetries and capture a dense subgroup in the
full SO(1, dph − 1) underlying continuous group?

Building off of the ideas in [2], the first step towards answering this question happened
in an MSc thesis [3], for which the author served as a co-supervisor (together with Latham
Boyle; see Statement of Contributions). In Section 9.1.1, we review the results of the
thesis, while in Section 9.1.2 we present our own ongoing work to extend these results.
The remaining of this chapter is devoted to adapting the CNP scheme to our new findings.
In Section 9.2 we give a more general sCNP scheme performed in the root basis (instead of
the Cartesian one). Finally, in Section 9.3 we put the algorithm to work to produce the
first-ever icosahedrally-symmetric (3 + 1)D spacetime quasicrystal.

9.1 Revisiting the Non-Crystallographic Symmetry

Constructing sCNP quasicrystals can be algebraically understood as searching for non-
crystallographic subgroups within crystallographic parent groups. Once we know that
such a Coxeter pair exists (see Section 6.2.3), then we can build a sCNP scheme starting
from the lattice whose symmetries are described by that parent group and obtain the
quasi-crystalline pattern with the desired non-crystallographic symmetry. In this chapter,
we refer to a (non-)crystallographic group as GC (GNC). A Coxeter pair is then denoted
as (GC , GNC).

As mentioned in that Section, all the possible Coxeter pairs are known for the Euclidean
cases. Interestingly, it is also known that for all these cases, the non-crystallographic
symmetry group GNC can be obtained by folding the crystallographic graph; to indicate

112



folding, we write GC ↠ GNC . Indeed, in Fig. 6.4 we encountered all the interesting non-
crystallographic foldings of the spherical Coxeter groups, such as E8 ↠ H4, D6 ↠ H3,
and the three 4D-to-2D sCNP schemes, A4 ↠ I52 , B4 ↠ I82 and F4 ↠ I122 (the three most
relevant symmetries of natural quasicrystals). Knowing the lattice (i.e. GC), the symmetry
GNC and, by extension, the window invariant under GNC (i.e. a 600-cell, an icosahedron,
a decagon, an octagon or a dodecagon respectively, see Section 6.2), one can just follow
the sCNP prescription of Section 7.2 to build the spatial quasicrystals.

On the other hand, even though several examples of non-crystallographic hyperbolic
Coxeter groups are known in the literature, it is not known if any of them can be embed-
ded into a higher-rank crystallographic group of the same nature to form a hyperbolic
Coxeter pair. Indeed, there are around 16 non-crystallographic graphs in Figs. 2 & 3
in [65] (most due to Lannér [150]), which exist only up to dimension d = 5 (and thus
tessellate the hyperboloid of dimension up to d − 1 = 4), but none of them is known to
exist as a subgroup of some appropriately higher-rank GC . This inhibits the construction
of any spacetime sCNP scheme to produce quasicrystals with these symmetry groups..

Despite these challenges, to make some progress and actually construct a spacetime qua-
sicrystal, we chose in Section 8.2 integer self-dual lattices and their GC ’s as the starting
point (Section 8.1.1). The reasoning was simple: the nicest spatial quasicrystals are con-
structed from such self-dual lattice, like E8 or B4 ≃ Z4 and A4 ↪→ Z5 for the Elser-Sloane
quasicrystal or the Ammann-Beenker and Penrose tilings respectively. Thus, mathemati-
cal elegance led us to the self-dual Lorentzian lattices Id−1,1 and IId−1,1 for d ≤ 10. All of
these graphs are bicolourable (see Fig. 8.1), which allowed us to consider the simplest GNC

inside them, or equivalently, the simplest non-crystallographic folding: grouping all red
and all blue generators together, one obtains an infinite dihedral group (8.8) characteristic
of each GC , as shown in Fig. 9.1. Geometrically, these foldings correspond to projections
onto the Coxeter planes and the resulting structures suffer from the issues mentioned in
the beginning of this chapter.

A natural question, then, is: can we fold the graphs of the self-dual integer lattices in
some other way to obtain more general GNC ’s? The answer turns out to be negative, and
we now turn to this topic in the next subsection. We reserve Appendix B for the details
regarding graph folding.

9.1.1 No Non-Crystallographic Foldings of Simplicial Hyperbolic
Coxeter Graphs

Central to the theory of spherical Coxeter pairs are the Coxeter elements: for the cases
identified in [5], for example, it is noted that the Coxeter number is shared between a Cox-
eter pair (GC , GNC). Additionally, in any dD-to-2D sCNP scheme, the Coxeter eigenbasis
indicates the subspaces on which to project a higher-rank lattice Λ (stabilized by GC) to
produce the quasi-crystalline pattern of lower-rank with symmetry GNC . In fact, this gen-
eralizes to any higher-dimensional sCNP scheme, as explained in Appendix B: for the sCNP
scheme based on the spherical Coxeter pair (E8, H4), for instance, the bicoloured Coxeter
eigenbasis tell us how to carry out the projection to get the Elser-Sloane H4-quasicrystal
and realize H4 as a subgroup of E8. As a result, one would reasonably expect that the
Coxeter elements would hold the key to understanding hyperbolic Coxeter pairs too. Af-
ter all, this led to all spacetime quasicrystals constructed so far, based on a Coxeter pair
(GC = Id−1,1 or IId−1,1,Dih∞).

114



Given a Coxeter pair (GC , GNC), which may be spherical or hyperbolic, there are two
equivalent ways to express this relationship between the two members: (1) the folding way
GC ↠ GNC , and (2) its “inverse”, the embedding way GNC ↪→ GC , or the “unfolding” way.
Here, we focus on viewpoint (1); viewpoint (2) will be discussed in the next subsection.

In the thesis [3], we formulated a necessary – but crucially not sufficient – condition
for some Coxeter graph H to arise as a folding of some other Coxeter graph G when both
of the graphs are irreducible and their graphs are trees (i.e. no loops). The idea is that if
H embeds in G by graph folding, then the eigenvalues of their respective Coxeter elements
CH and CG must be related as spec(CH) ⊆ spec(CG). We focus on trees because then
it makes sense to talk about the Coxeter element and the spectrum. In other words, if
rank(G) = rG and rank(H) = rH , the rH eigenvalues of the rH×rH folded Coxeter element
CH must be drawn from the pool of the rG eigenvalues of the original rG × rG Coxeter
element CG. We call this the eigenvalue-sharing condition [3]; we give a more precise
statement in Lemma 1 in Appendix B, together with some examples.

Using this condition, we were able to show the following:

• No Hyperbolic Coxeter Pairs Between Simplicial Trees [3]: considering all
simplicial hyperbolic graphs from [65, 134] that do not contain any closed circuits,
we were unable to find any two of them that satisfy the eigenvalue-sharing condition.
This shows that it is impossible to embed any known hyperbolic tree-like1 GNC into
some crystallographic partner GC of the same properties, i.e. tree-like, simplicial and
with only spherical or affine subgraphs. This theorem is proven by exhaustion using
the known classification of simplicial hyperbolic Coxeter groups and a Python script
that checked the eigenvalue-sharing condition against all these graphs. The script
and more details about it are available in [3].

– A particular subcase of this theorem is that our integer self-dual lattices GC =
Id−1,1 or IId−1,1 (d ≤ 10) contain no known GNC either.

• A Non-Simplicial Candidate for a Hyperbolic Coxeter Pair [3]: relaxing the
condition for simplicial fundamental domains, we also considered four more tree-like
graphs, those of Id−1,1 for 11 ≤ d ≤ 14 shown in Fig. D.1 from Vinberg’s classifica-
tion [148]. We found that a non-crystallographic hyperbolic Coxeter group from the
simplicial classification [65], known as L353 [134], whose graph is

5

shares its eigenvalues with the crystallographic I13,1, though we were unable to

As a natural next step to extend these results, it would be interesting to include those

Another idea would be to check if a given non-crystallographic graph – from either the

not included in the known classifications. We have tried certain examples with no luck
and we discuss these findings in Appendix B. Before thinking of ways to extend the search
deeper into the unknown, though, we have found another method to define hyperbolic
Coxeter pairs, as we know explain.

9.1.2 Unfolding Non-Crystallographic Simplicial Hyperbolic Cox-
eter Graphs Into Crystallographic Graphs

We now take viewpoint (2) of understanding Coxeter pairs: instead of trying to fold a given
GC into some also known GNC , we start from a desired non-crystallographic member GNC

and attempt to lift it to some higher-rank lattice whose stabilizer is GC . Stated differently,
for a given GNC , our goal it to embed – or “unfold” – it into some GC ; we write GNC ↪→ GC .

To that end, we devised a method capable of unfolding all spherical non-crystallographic
groups into their corresponding crystallographic counterparts; the details are explained in
Appendix B and a sketch of the method is given below. We then applied the method to
unfold certain simplicial GNC of particular interest to their crystallographic parent groups.
This way, we constructed a first list of the long-sought hyperbolic Coxeter pairs shown in
Fig. B.5 and B.6 in Appendix B.2.2.

116



The idea is very simple, but it requires some amount of algebraic number theory (see
Appendix A). In its simplest form, it goes as follows: consider a Coxeter graph and con-
struct its Schläfli matrix S from it according to Eq. (6.19). The entries will belong to
some number field K: if the graph is crystallographic, the number field will be just the
rationals K = Q. 2; if the graph is non-crystallographic, we get some rational extension
R by some irrationality. When the degree of K over R is 2, we can represent any element
of SNC by a 2× 2 rational matrix, leading to a graph in twice as many dimensions that is
crystallographic (see Appendix B).

A very interesting non-crystallographic group from the simplicial classification [65] is
the group L353 we encountered in the previous subsection, the one that shares eigenvalues
with I13,1. Its graph resembles F4 from the Euclidean classification of Fig. 6.1, but instead of
the label 4 in its middle two nodes it has a 5. Because of this, its Schläfli matrix becomes
indefinite; we call it HF4 (hyperbolic F4). This makes HF4 very interesting because it
contains a maximal finite icosahedral Coxeter subgroup H3, as one can verify by removing
either node from its ends. Using our unfolding techniques, we can embed the rank-4 HF4

group into a lattice in twice as much dimensions whose crystallographic symmetry group
is the 8-node graph HE+

7 , as shown in Fig. 9.2. We call it HE+
7 (hyperbolic extended E7)

because it is an extended (by one node) version of the finite E7 graph of Fig. 6.1: removing
node 2 or 8 gives back the familiar E7.

This resulting rank-8 crystallographic graph belongs to no known classification [65,
148]. The reason for this is that it contains hyperbolic subgraphs and thus ultra-ideal
vertices (see Section 6.2.1), which makes its fundamental domain acquire infinite volume.
For example, removing node 4 from HE+

7 , one gets back a simplicial rank-7 hyperbolic
graph that is included in the list of [65]. Nevertheless, it is a valid graph – its Schläfli
matrix has the correct (7, 1) signature – and defines a perfectly valid root lattice in M8.

Icosahedrally symmetric patterns exhibit three types of rotational symmetries: (i) 2-
fold, (ii) 3-fold and, (iii) 5- or 10-fold. Indeed, a regular icosahedron {3, 3, 5} has: six
5-fold axes (passing through the 12 opposite vertices; rotations around vertices where 5
triangular faces meet, mapping one face to another), ten 3-fold axes (passing through the
centres of the 20 opposite triangular faces; rotations map the three vertices of each face
to one another), and fifteen 2-fold axes (passing through the midpoints of the 30 edges of
the icosahedron; reflects the endpoints of each edge). These 31 axes generate 60 rotational
symmetries, which are combined with a reflection, to yield the full H3 group of order 120.

10.1 Fitting the Universe in a Nutshell

Superstring theory [203, 204, 39, 40] has been much-studied as a candidate unified theory;
but mathematical consistency requires the superstring to live in a (9+1) dimensional target
space to cancel the worldsheet Weyl anomaly.

To reconcile this with the (3+1) dimensional universe we observe, the standard approach
is to imagine (a modern variant of) the Kaluza-Klein picture in which four of the ten
dimensions are large and non-compact, while the remaining six “extra” spatial dimensions
are “compactified” (i.e. curled up into an unobservably tiny 6D compact manifold). Alas,
this picture so far does not have any observational evidence in its favour, and arguably
creates more problems than its solves. In particular, stabilizing the six extra dimensions in
a way that agrees with observations has been a notoriously difficult, and has driven theorists
to consider awkwardly complex mechanisms that are often compared to Rube-Goldberg
machines, and lead to a vast “string landscape” of possible vacua for 4D spacetime.

131



Here we propose a new geometric picture for how our 4D universe might be embedded in
a higher-dimensional spacetime, completely different from the usual Kaluza-Klein picture.
Although our proposal is logically independent of string theory, superstrings provides an
intriguing motivation, as we now explain.

10.1.1 Classical Picture: Irrational Spacetime

The most well studied compactifications of string theory are the toroidal compactifications:
here one takes m of the target-space dimensions to be curled up in an m-dimensional torus
Tm, which is constructed by taking m-dimensional flat space Rm modulo an m-dimensional
lattice Λm: Tm = Rm/Λm. Due to stringy effects (in particular T -duality [205]), such
compactifications can have much higher symmetry than one would naively expect based
on the isometry group of the compactified target spacetime. In [133], Moore studied such
toroidal compactifications in generality, including the possibility of compactifying the time
direction! He found that the most symmetric toroidal compactification of the superstring
was obtained when all 10 dimensions of the target space were compactified on the 10D
Lorentzian torus T9,1 constructed by taking 10D Minkowski space R9,1 modulo the 10D
even self-dual Lorentzian lattice Λ9,1: T9,1 = R9,1/II9,1.

This most-symmetric superstring compactification was assumed to be unphysical, and
of purely academic interest, for two reasons: first, because if all ten dimensions are com-
pactified at an ultra-microscopic scale, then one seems to be left without any remaining
non-compact directions to serve as the (3 + 1) macroscopic directions we observe; and
second, because all directions (including time) are compactified, then the target spacetime
has closed time-like curves which are usually assumed to be pathological, since they seem
to be paradoxical and at odds with the causality properties of our universe.

However, the previous section’s spacetime quasicrystal construction suggests a way
around this conclusion.

11.1 Causal Set Theory: a Brief Overview

Causal Set Theory (CST) is an approach to quantum gravity where spacetime discrete-

Therefore, the Poisson process, and the discrete random geometries it carries with it, is
central to the CST hypothesis. But is this as good as it gets?

Why Random Instead of Ordered?

Before we answer, let us briefly mention some desirable features of the Poisson process that
one would reasonably expect also for any other point process.

• Lorentz Invariance. Going back to the discussion about Lorentz covariance, it has
been shown [213] that any random causet coming from a Poisson sprinkling does not
break Lorentz symmetry in Minkowski spacetime4, as one cannot consistently pick a
direction throughout spacetime that singles out any particular frame (see also §3.2
in [38]). This implies that, if ΦPoisson(C) is a uniform distribution in (M, ηµν) in
some frame, then it will be also uniform with respect to any other frame. In a sense,
the Poisson process respects Lorentz symmetry, not by actually preserving it at the
level of the discrete causal set, but by having randomness prevent the selection of
preferred frames. This way one recovers (local) Lorentz invariance at the continuous
approximation, which is a property we would want for any point process Φ, as Lorentz
invariance seems to withstand any experimental test so far [214, 215, 216].

Letting aside questions about generality for the moment, let us first focus on the fol-

numbers to volumes in Minkowski spacetime except for Poisson?

Perhaps a regular – ordered – structure, a lattice in Minkowski spacetime, can do
the trick. After all, its translational symmetry is enough to make it uniform in its rest
frame; the whole pattern is governed by a single repeating fundamental cell, what else can
look more uniform that this? Fig. (11.2) shows what goes wrong with the integer lattice

appears regular and uniform in its rest frame, it becomes irregular and non-uniform for a
boosted observer (squeezed in the boost-direction and stretched in the perpendicular one).
This implies that such structures lead to a poor number-volume realization, and we will
revisit this to see exactly what fails in the next subsection.

If randomness beats regularity then, can we extend the theorem from [211] and show
that Poisson sprinklings actually beat everything across all ranges of scales? The answer
turns out to be no: for ⟨N♦⟩ > 1, the proof fails, as is noted in their work. And before one
starts scheming of other methods to make Poisson stand out again, the authors have found a
counterexample: perhaps surprisingly, a lattice in (1+1)-dimensional Minkowski spacetime
with discrete Lorentz symmetry has been found to realize the N-V correspondence much
better than Poisson at large scales (effectively, for any macroscopic volume ρV♦ ≥ 1) [211].
Given that we have found a new class of ordered5 causal sets in this thesis, our spacetime
quasicrystals, which also have discrete Lorentz symmetry, we should test them against the
traditional random causal sets and the lattices and quantify if and how well they satisfy
the N-V correspondence.

In the following subsections, we run the N-V test for several point sets in (1 + n)-
dimensional Minkowski spacetime for n = 1, 2 and 3. We replicate the results from [211]
in (1 + 1)D, which is our main reference on this matter, while also adding some of our
spacetime quasicrystals in the analysis. Then, we continue on higher dimensions and we
test their conjecture in (3 + 1)D. We reserve the Appendix F for some details regarding
the tests. As we shall see, we provide evidence that their conjecture does not hold, and
our spacetime quasicrystals could actually beat Poisson in the N-V test.

pattern). If ϖ ∈ [kϖsym, (k+1)ϖsym] for some Z ∋ k ≥ 1, then the previous changes of the
pattern repeat: two boosted patterns by rapidities ϖ and ϖ + ϖsym are the same (up to
labelling of points). Now, imagine that some higher-dimensional pattern has independent
boost symmetries along, let’s say, all three directions x, y and z, given by some parameters
ϖsym,x, ϖsym,y and ϖsym,z. Even if the pattern does not change ‘too much’ for a boost in
the t-x plane, there is still ‘plenty of room’ to boost in any of the other planes and distort
the pattern till we reach the values ϖsym,y or ϖsym,z. An even better scenario would be that
the pattern under consideration has also high rotational symmetries that can mix the three
independent planes, leading to even more symmetric boost directions. For a Lorentzian
lattice, the rotational symmetries are limited by the crystallographic restriction theorem,
but a quasicrystal avoids this and can show more intricate symmetries. In these cases, a
dense set of symmetric boost directions is expected to exist, like for the HF4-quasicrystal
of Section 9.3.1, and the spacetime quasicrystals will absorb most boosts.

Since our spacetime quasicrystals satisfy the requirements of the Poisson’s demise con-
jecture in any dimension, they are promising candidates to outperform sprinklings in higher
dimensions as well.

directions along the plane!), while in (1 + 3)D there are three, ϖx, ϖy and ϖz, including boosts in the t-y
and t-z planes as well.

In condensed-matter physics, structures whose number variance grows slower than that
of Poisson-random structures (i.e. slower than the volume of some observation window,
which for our purposes is given by ♦) are called hyperuniform [220]. This gives us an
entry point in understanding more formally the results of the N-V test, together with an

11.3.1 Direct-Space Variance, Euclidean Spatial Statistics and the
First Definition of Hyperuniformity

First, we need to understand to a certain extent what hyperuniformity is in the Euclidean
context, which is where the concept was originally developed. The main reference here is
the review [220] and the seminal work [221], to which we point the reader for details; we
also found this presentation material by Torquato useful in writing this section.

Hyperuniformity is a property that led to a new classification and structural charac-
terization of matter, including ordered structures – crystals, quasicrystals – but also more
exotic disordered point configurations [221]. States of matter with this property are cor-
related systems characterized by strong suppression of large-scale (i.e. long-wavelength)
density fluctuations, which does not occur for usual disordered systems such as ordinary
fluids (e.g. ideal gases, liquids) and amorphous solids (e.g. glasses). The origins of this
behaviour can be traced back to how the variance grows with the geometric properties of
some observational patch.

Imagine a point pattern P in d-dimensional Euclidean space Rd; the points could rep-
resent atoms of a physical material, points of a mathematical structure, like a periodic
lattice or an aperiodic quasicrystal, or stars in some galaxy far, far away. Let Ω be some
observation window over the pattern, i.e. we probe P by placing a patch Ω on it and
looking only at those points inside Ω. The shape of Ω could be any convex set, and if the
point process has certain symmetries, Ω can be chosen to be adapted to those. A con-
venient choice, though, especially for statistically isotropic point sets in Euclidean space,
is a (hyper-)spherical window whose geometric parameter is only its radius R [221, 220].
By sampling many such patches Ω over P and collecting the statistics, one can calculate
the average number of points inside Ω, ⟨NΩ(R)⟩, and the associated local number variance

Mathematically, ρg2(r)ddr measures the conditional probability of finding a point (“a

usually taken to be (hyper)spherical, but one could consider some angle-dependent volumes

at exactly distance r away?’. For completely uncorrelated point sets, like random Poisson
structures without any long-range order, g2(r) = 1 for all arguments and h(r) vanishes
identically [221].13 The explanation here is that for a random structure there is always
a probability that one will find a neighbour at any scale, as any distance can appear on
a random pattern. On the other hand, for an ordered structure, only certain distances
can appear ; for example, for a lattice point configuration, the nearest neighbour will be a
lattice-spacing away, so g2(r) vanishes for distances lower than that, but picks up a sharp

see Fig. 11.10). Based on this, we note the following cases; the interpretations are to be
taken against a random structure:

• g(r) = 1: equal probability of finding a neighbour at any distance r (randomness),

• g(r) > 1: higher probability of finding a neighbour at distance r; pairs of points at
distance r are more abundant than the spatial average (clustering).

• g(r) < 1: lower probability of finding a neighbour at distance r; pairs of points at
distance r are less abundant than the spatial average (dispersion/exclusion)

11.3.5 Towards a Lorentz-invariant Hyperuniformity Estimator?

We close the section about spacetime hyperuniformity by mentioning a couple thoughts
about how to extend the results of the previous section in a more Lorentz-invariant frame-
work.

First, for the spatial statistics measures of Section 11.3.3, an idea would be to calculate
the pair correlation function g2(r) on a Lorentzian point set not by drawing spheres (Eu-
clidean invariant) but causal diamonds instead. For example, we could fix the centre of
some ♦ on a point of the pattern and draw causal diamonds of increasing proper time away
from that centre; then, we could calculate the spacelike and timelike distances of all points
included in the causal diamonds. Having both negative and positive spacetime distances
would make the interpretation of figure like Fig. 11.10c difficult, however it would be more
in the spirit of Lorentz-invariance.

Second, as mentioned before, our formulas so far – like Eq. (11.30) for (k♦)min – depend
only on the magnitude of the wavenumber; equal volumes V♦, no matter how boosted they
are, will give the same k♦. It is clear that, in order to properly consider a hyperuniformity
estimator in (3+1)D, for example, where boosts carry direction dependence on S2, we would
need to find a way to factor that in. Also, in our definition of spacetime hyperuniformity
(Eq. (11.21) and related formulas), what matters is the behaviour of the structure factor
as the magnitude of the wavenumber k goes to zero, independent of k’s directional degrees
of freedom. This has been generalized in [232] to account for anisotropic spectral densities.
Perhaps this is relevant for us here; we leave this for future work.

11.4 Phenomenology and Future Directions in qCST

It is rather tempting to close this section on causal set theory – or its quasi-crystalline
version – by offering some very speculative ideas about some interesting physics one could
do with spacetime quasicrystals. Normally, these would belong to Chapter 12 with the
rest of the speculative ideas, but since they do refer to causal set theory more directly, we
decided to give them here.

11.4.1 Spectral Graph Properties

Graph observables have been shown to be very powerful in distinguishing between differ-
ent causal sets [212, 233] (the last reference treated also our I3,1 spacetime quasicrystal).

184



While random causal sets have no inherent structure (and thus their graph properties are
not analytically understood), we can analytically study the underlying graphs of ordered
structures easier. Ultimately, the goal is to get a more graph-theoretic understanding of
how to build, let’s say, an action for causal sets from objects inherent to the causal set, or
how to describe operators on a causal set, or how to quantify the entropy of a causal set.

Propagators and Graph Laplacians

We know from the work of [234] that certain graph-observables, like the adjacency matrix
of a graph, are related to field propagators (Green’s functions) on a causal set (see also §5
in [38]). For example, in (1 + 1)D, the causal propagator ∆ is given as i∆ = GR − GA =

living on a causal set C, and C is the adjacency matrix of C. Recently, the eigenvalues
of this object in various dimensions have captured some attention in the literature [235],
and conjectures have been formulated about their asymptotic behaviours. It would be
interesting to calculate the spectrum of these operators on a spacetime quasicrystal – a
quasi-crystalline causet C – and compare to that of a traditional causet.

In the spirit of understanding better how to build propagators from a causal set (and
not by taking a field on a causal set and matching its propagators to quantities of C, as done

study discrete Green’s functions G, solutions to the equation LG = 1, where L is the graph
Laplacian and 1 here is a unit matrix of appropriate dimensions. This is in analogy to
the continuous Green’s functions, which are solutions to □GR/A(x, x

Since □ is the “square” of the Dirac operator D and L is the “square” of B, one can try to

BG = 1 would give fermionic propagators (for fields satisfying the Dirac equation). It
would be interesting to see what kind of G’s we get for a spacetime quasicrystal.

Point-Set Correlations and Intrinsic Spacetime Entanglement

Usually, when we consider the entanglement entropy of a system (i.e. a quantum field) on
spacetime, we do not say that the underlying spacetime is itself entangled. Similarly, when

185



we deal with quantum fields on a fixed causal set (like in [234, 239, 240]), we calculate
the entanglement entropy of that field on some C, and there is no contribution there from
C itself. However, if C is itself a quantum description of spacetime, could it have some
intrinsic spacetime entanglement?

In [241], a density matrix was constructed for any given graph, and some of its properties
were studied. Thinking of C as a graph, we can use these techniques to assign a density
matrix to C. We can then attempt to calculate the spacetime entanglement entropy between
a spacetime region (i.e. a subset of our causet C) and its complement by tracing out the
complement. Could it be that this process leads to different results for a traditional and
a quasi-crystalline causet? Can we use the intrinsic non-trivial long-range correlations
inherent to a spacetime quasicrystal (see Section 11.3.3) to encode this intrinsic spacetime
entanglement (i.e. connectivity between its different patches)? If so, this would provide
new insights into the “entanglement builds geometry” paradigm, usually emphasized in
holographic contexts [242].

Chapter 12

Further Connections of Spacetime
Quasicrystals to Physics

In this last Chapter, let us end by briefly mentioning some other connections of spacetime
quasicrystals to physics, as interesting topics for future investigations.

12.1 In Computational Complexity Theory

Scale-symmetric quasicrystals, in particular the Ammann-Beenker tilings, have recently
shown to be efficient in solving the general-case NP-complete problem of finding Hamilto-
nian cycles (i.e. closed loops on a graph visiting each vertex precisely once) [247]. Since
many interesting problems in physics fall in the NP complexity class, this result hints
towards the fact that quasicrystals are essentially as powerful (if not more) as periodic
lattices in simplifying certain physical problems. It would be interesting to understand the
graph-theoretic properties of spacetime quasicrystals and see what kind of problems their
special properties can help us solve.

12.2 In Various Discretizations

Given their discrete scale invariance, quasicrystals provide natural mathematical structures
on which to discretize and study systems in which (exact or approximate) scale or conformal

189



invariance plays an important role (e.g. QFTs near their fixed points, condensed matter
systems near their critical points, or our universe near the Big Bang).

We mention two interesting ideas:

• Fermions on a Lattice: (chiral) fermions are notoriously difficult to be placed
on a lattice without doubling the degrees of freedom (thus the fermion doubling
problem). This is formalized in the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem, a no-go theorem
telling us that, under locality, hermiticity, and translational symmetry, any attempt
to place a chiral fermion on a lattice (let’s say, a right-handed one), necessarily
leads to an equal number of left-handed and right-handed fermions on the lattice
(see [248, 249, 250, 251]). However, perhaps fermion discretizations on non-periodic
(spacetime) quasicrystals could avoid the doubling problem (by going around no-go
theorem since there is no translational invariance).

• Anderson Localization: condensed-matter analogues are ubiquitous in high-energy
theory (like the Higgs mechanism), and Anderson localization [252] is another very
interesting one. Effectively, this refers to inhibition of wave propagation and con-
finement of eigenstates (as opposed to delocalized Bloch electrons shared among all
atoms in a material), and can occur either because of randomness (as in the original
paper [252]) or because of a quasi-random, quasi-periodic potential [253, 254, 255].
It is known, for example, that, while random and uncorrelated potentials perfectly
localize electrons in materials (the decay of a wavefunction is exponential), quasi-
periodic potentials lead to a scale-invariant, power-law localization.
It would be interesting to explore how something like this manifests on a spacetime
quasicrystal. Here, the role of wavefunctions in materials is played by quantum
fields living on spacetime. The role of the potential is less clear, but an intriguing
scenario would be to consider whether the quasi-periodicity of the geometric structure
itself is enough to lead to the emergence of localized excitations (i.e. particles) from
fundamental quantum fields (delocalized states), if one discretizes the fields on a
spacetime quasicrystal.
Relatedly, it has been shown that the return probability of walks on a graph (start-
ing from some initial site and returning back to it after, let’s say, N moves) plays
a role for transient behaviours of statistical models or Anderson localization in dis-
ordered solids (see [256] and references in their introduction). Treating spacetime
quasicrystal as causal sets and considering their underlying graph structure would
be a promising start to investigate if they have localization properties (by studying
the return probability of walks on them), which might also relate to the Hamiltonian
cycles problem mentioned before.

190



12.3 In String Theory, Particle Physics, and Cosmology

There may be interesting connections between the compactification scenario we suggest in
Secs. 10.1.1, 10.2.1, 10.2.2 and the “quasicrystalline string compactifications” idea discussed
in [51, 52]. It shall be noted, however, that the two approaches seem to have a different
starting point. While the latter is an orbifold-type compactification (operating at the level
of the string world-sheet where the string’s left- and right-going modes live), our construc-
tion is a string target-space compactification (i.e. it compactifies the 10D target space on
a 10D lattice). For this reason, we view our method as a new class of compactifications
that employ “forbidden” non-crystallographic symmetries distinct from quasi-crystalline
orbifolds, which could realize Moore’s [133] original idea.

Another approach in string theory potentially related to our work is the much-studied
IKKT matrix model of Type IIB string theory. This may also be thought of as arising from
D=10 super Yang-Mills theory, by compactifying all 10 dimensions of spacetime down to
a point [257, 258]. Since our compactified space is a 10D torus and E10 is an infinite group
appearing frequently in supergravity, it is natural to explore whether the resulting infinite
matrices recover the IKKT model in the limit where our torus shrinks to a point.

Finally, our compactification scenario (based on compactifying 10D spacetime using the
II9,1 = E10 root lattice) might have connections to other investigations of the role of E10

in string theory, cosmology and the standard model [163, 164, 165, 166, 167]. One poten-
tially interesting observation in particle physics could be the following1: could the discrete
symmetry of spacetime quasicrystals somehow account for the new intriguing pattern in
the Yukawa couplings observed in [259]? In particular, their Fig. 3 of the distribution
of angles for the rephasing-invariant CP violating phase φ with peaks at angles multiples
of π/8 is reminiscent of our Fig. 9.4, which could emerge for a π/8-symmetric (instead of
π/5-symmetric) spacetime quasicrystal. On that same topic of angular distributions, there
are also works showing a preference for icosahedral symmetry of CMB-correlations in the
sky [260, 261, 262]; it would be nice if those can be explained by spacetime’s underlying
aperiodic order.

12.4 In Quantum Error Correction

Spacetime quasicrystals may yield new insights into the recently noticed, but still incom-
pletely understood, triangle of connections between (discrete) holography (an approach to

quantum gravity) and quantum error correction [242], between quantum error correction
and quasicrystals [76], and between quasicrystals and (discrete) holography [77, 69]. We
refer to this affectionately as the Q-Triangle in Fig. 12.1.

In particular, in [76] it was shown that the Penrose tiling is a particular type of quan-
tum error-correcting code, or QECC for short. QECCs offer a way to store quantum
information with some redundancy so that it can be efficiently recovered if corrupted [82].
Schematically, the relation between QECCs and quasicrystals (QCs) is based on two prin-
ciples:

• Local indistinguishability, on the side of the quasicrystals (see Section 7.3.1), provides
the needed redundancy for encoding information (there are infinitely many quasi-
crystalline patches that are locally the same but globally different, so locally one
cannot say with certainty in which patch they are).

• Recoverability, or reconstructability, allows then for error-correction. This is a prop-
erty of quasicrystals that allows us to rebuild any missing patch from the pattern by
inspecting the local neighbourhood only, without needing global information.

We call this the QECC-QC dictionary. While the first property follows almost directly
from the irrationality of the CNP slice for a quasicrystal, the second is less trivial to have,
and indeed we are unsure how to extend it to the spacetime quasicrystals. This is because
recoverability becomes possible either by using local scale invariance (see Section 7.3.5),

192



or the so-called Ammann-lines [5]. Our spacetime quasicrystals lack the first property
(see Section 8.3), and we did not yet think carefully about whether our patterns admit
Ammann-lines.

Nevertheless, this does not stop us from imagining what would be the case if spacetime
had quasi-crystalline structure. Could it be this gives rise to a quantum error-correcting
spacetime? Perhaps before we even go there, it would undoubtedly be an interesting
question to show whether and what type of QECCs spacetime quasicrystals generate.

12.5 In Quantum Gravity: Bridging Different Approaches

Spacetime quasicrystals may be of interest in studying quantum gravity, as explicit, mathe-
matically natural models for discretized spacetime, with many interesting, non-trivial, and
counterintuitive properties, and a high degree of (orientational and scale) symmetry (and
quasi-symmetry).

In particular, they provide a novel class of causal sets, as we discussed explicitly in
Chapter 11, very different from either Lorentzian lattices or random sets [233]. In Sections
11.2 and 11.3, we provided concrete evidence that our quasi-crystalline causal sets are good
models (in the sense of the N-V test) for discrete spacetime. In Section 11.4, we provided
several speculative ideas about how they might relate to physics.

Due to their discrete scale invariance, spacetime quasicrystals may be especially rele-
vant to quantum gravity approaches where spacetime has a fractal, scale-invariant char-
acter (e.g. asymptotic safety [263, 264, 41, 265]). Interestingly, the suggest a way to tie
the “discretum” and the “continuum”. Finite-density spacetime quasicrystals are discrete
yet preserve much of the underlying continuous Lorentz symmetry. To recover full (global)
scale-symmetry, though, we need a countable but dense quasicrystal, which better approxi-
mates the continuous and scale-symmetric fractal spacetime of Asymptotic Safety. Indeed,
the asymptotic safety community is very interested in understanding the configuration
space of all possible causal sets [233]. This is because they are searching for a rationale for
asymptotic safety, which tells us that gravity has a UV fixed-point close to which scale-
symmetry kicks in. Perhaps this can be understood as arising from a second-order phase
transition in the space of all possible causal sets, similar to how a quantum system exhibits
scale-symmetry and universality close to its fixed points. To that end, perhaps adding the
scale-invariant spacetime quasicrystals is helpful.

Another key question is whether quasi-crystalline causets admit natural (aperiodic)
tessellations and what could be their “fundamental geometric atoms”. In Section 8.3, we

193



concluded that a tiling that respects the non-crystallographic symmetry is probably impos-
sible in Lorentzian space, so we would need to consider different types of tessellations. To
that end, one could leverage the graph-theoretic properties of spacetime quasicrystals to
develop algorithms that connect points to form tiles, thus finding their ‘geometric atoms’.
This will add a novel alternative to Euclidean distance-based tessellation methods, like
Voronoi’s algorithm [61], which fail in Lorentzian geometry because of the indefiniteness
of the metric. If a tessellation exists that also preserves all (or even, some) symmetry, this
could provide a new way to generate highly ordered and symmetric spacetime triangula-
tions, which could bridge (quasi-crystalline) CST with the CDT-approach.

All these potential applications of spacetime quasicrystals in quantum gravity enhance
the known connections described at the Q-Triangle of Fig. 12.1. Indeed, so far all quantum-
gravity applications were holographic, as mentioned in the previous section. In this thesis,
for the first time, we point out several structural parallels between different approaches to
quantum gravity that are certainly worth to be pursued more in our opinion.

Chapter 13

Outlook

In this final short Chapter, we take some time to remind the reader of the main two points
we would like to get across from Part I and Part II of this thesis.

13.1 Computation at the Core of Physics?

In Part I, we argued that two research fields that are perceived as rather disparate, namely
computational complexity theory in computer science and (quantum) gravitational physics
in theoretical physics, are actually closer than one might think. The connection, as empha-
sized in Chapter 2, is simply something that no physical theory can escape: computation
is a physical process, and the physical laws tell us what is efficiently computable.

The distinction between efficiently computable (P) and efficiently verifiable (NP) is the
essence of the P ?

= NP problem. Experience suggests that these two complexity classes
cannot be the same: coming up with creative new proofs must be harder than verifying one
that is already available. Mathematically, this statement is the physical extended Church-
Turing thesis (PECTT), which tell us that no physical device, no matter how powerful,
can efficiently solve NP. And this is exactly what all of our physical theories, including
theories about gravity and the quantum world, shall respect.

A classical or a quantum computer abides by the classical or quantum laws of physics
when it processes information and manipulates (qu)bits in order to perform tasks. This
is a physical process, governed by a set of physical laws, and thus must conform to the
PECTT. Of course, the classical set of laws is included within the quantum set, so we
expect a computational speed-up for the quantum computer. But if the PECTT is right,

195



this would not be enough to solve NP efficiently. Similarly, a “(quantum) gravitational
computer” functions through a very different set of physical laws, but it remains a physical
device as much as its classical or quantum version.1 As such, it must also adhere to the
PECTT, and any computational advantage from it must be modest.

In Chapter 5, we propose that the PECTT shall become part of the axioms of our
physical theories. We used this criterion to argue – in Section 4 – that semiclassical
gravity violates the PECTT and thus must not be a fundamental description of how gravity
behaves. Since this is the most popular alternative to quantum gravity (which keeps the
gravitational field completely classical instead of quantizing it in some way), we interpreted
our results as an argument in favour of quantum gravity. At the end of the day, the message
is clear: computational complexity theory has a lot to say about our physical theories.

13.2 The Role of Aesthetics in Pure and Applied Quan-
tum Gravity Research

“The Role of Aesthetics in Pure and Applied Mathematical Research”

Roger Penrose in his iconic paper [55] introducing the Penrose tilings

Historically, quasicrystals are very interesting because they started from the world of
recreational mathematics [54, 56, 168], where people were thinking of different ways to tile
a plane. Imagine an infinite table and an endless supply of puzzle pieces. Your task: cover
the surface perfectly—no gaps, no overlaps—and yet never forming a pattern that repeats,
no matter how far you go. How many distinct shapes would you need? In 1961, Wang [266]
conjectured that it is impossible, until his student, Berger, showed in 1966 [267] that there
exist a set of 20426 such “dominoes” that does the trick. By 1974, Penrose had dramatically
reduced the number to just two [55], a “kite” and a “dart” (Fig. 1.1). Yet it took another 50
years—and one more shape-hobbyist, the retired printing-technician David Smith—for the
“einstein” (German for “one stone” and a nod to a famous physicist) to do the impossible:
to find a single tile that fills the plane aperiodically all by itself [268, 269]!

1Of course, the author can use a classical computer to type this thesis, or visit the closest centre where
a quantum computer is being built and inspect it, but holding a quantum gravitational computer that
employs gravity to perform tasks is probably beyond even the wildest imagination. In any case, gravity is
a physical theory, and it gives rise to systems that can use this physical theory to compute something, in
the most abstract sense.

196



Nice patterns have always fascinated us because they are aesthetically pleasant. Roger
Penrose’s original work [55] introducing the Penrose tilings contains aesthetics in its title,
appreciating that aesthetics brings nice mathematics. Indeed, quasicrystals are not only
pleasant to the eye but carry a lot of beautiful mathematics with them, from lattices and
algebraic number theory, to discrete algebra, Fourier analysis and measure theory. In the
1980s, they even found their way to our labs, becoming the blueprints for a new form of
matter (see Chapter 1.3), thus moving from the mathematical to the physical world. This
discovery revolutionized how we thought about crystallography and what we considered as
“impossible” [75].

In Part II, we discussed a natural extension of quasicrystals from space to spacetime,
providing the first Lorentzian cousins of the Penrose tilings: spacetime quasicrystals. And
like this, quasicrystals made their way for the first time into the realm of relativistic
physics. This discovery opens an entirely new – and likely very rich – area of inquiry,
establishing a novel crossroads between crystallography, discrete geometry and algebraic
number theory on the one hand-side, and quantum gravity, quantum error-correction and
discrete conformal symmetry on the other.

Indeed, this thesis points out a vastly unexplored class of string-compactifications that
employ “forbidden” symmetries distinct from [52], and suggests a geometric seesaw expla-
nation for the large hierarchies among fundamental energy scales. It also hints at several
exciting applications of spacetime quasicrystals in other approaches to quantum gravity,
including in causal set theory (as highly-symmetric and highly-ordered alternatives to ran-
dom causal sets), in asymptotic safety (as point sets with discrete scale invariance), and as
a way of making concrete the belief that ‘quantum gravity is a quantum error-correction
code’ (since quasicrystals are quantum error correcting codes [76]).

From a quasi-crystalline lens, there are several intricate connections between quantum
gravity theories, as mentioned in Section 12.5 and throughout this thesis. But perhaps
even more interestingly, spacetime quasicrystals import new tools from condensed matter
physics and from algebraic number theory and discrete geometry into the realm of quantum
gravity. The concept of spacetime hyperuniformity, developed in Section 11.3, is a new
way of understanding the N-V test (Section 11.2) in causal set theory, and the algebraic
Wick rotation by a Galois-automorphism (Section 9.2.2) is perhaps a new way to transform
between a Euclidean and Lorentzian representation.

Could aesthetics play a role in the next breakthrough in quantum gravity? We do not
know, but taken all together, our work introduces spacetime quasicrystals as a qualitatively
new paradigm for spacetime discreteness that may reshape how we think about geometry,
information, and the quantum structure of spacetime.

While (algebraic) number theory may initially seem like pure mathematical abstraction,
it provides the rigorous machinery for classifying discrete symmetries of periodic and ape-
riodic lattices and related algebraic structures. This appendix outlines some necessary
formalism, with an emphasis on mapping numbers to the geometric language of lattices
and projections.

A.1 Some Notes on Algebraic Number Theory

Here we briefly introduce a few basic definitions, ideas and results in algebraic number
theory, which will be useful below. For more details, see Refs. [66, 67, 68] for standard
introductions to algebraic number theory. For our purposes, the first few chapters of [59]
are also very useful.

A.1.1 Preliminary Definitions

A field is a commutative ring in which the additive identity 0 and the multiplicative
identity 1 are distinct, and any non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse.1 Classic
examples are the rational numbers Q, the real numbers R, and the complex numbers C.

|Gal(K/Q)| = dK = [K : Q].

A.1.2 Symmetries, Subfields and Towers of Fields

Let K be a splitting field over Q. An automorphism σ : K → K is a bijective field
homomorphism that fixes the base field element-wise (i.e., σ(q) = q for all q ∈ Q). The set

corresponds to a symmetry group Gal(K/F ).

A.1.3 Extensions by Cyclotomic or Salem Numbers: Spherical vs
Hyperbolic

As mentioned already, the finite Coxeter groups with their finite-order h Coxeter element C
always give rise to a cyclotomic field Q(ζh). This is because the eigenvalues of C are always
the primitive h-th roots of unit, and come in complex-conjugate pairs (Section 6); these
always belong on S1 and are all complex. On the other hand, though, a hyperbolic Coxeter
element’s eigenvalues also come in pairs but crucially, there is a real pair associated with
a Salem number (see Section 8.1.3). This drastically changes some structural properties of
the associated field extensions.

Salem numbers θ are real algebraic integers greater than 1 whose other Galois conjugates
consist of 1/θ and pairs of complex-conjugate eigenvalues lying on S1; their relevance for
Coxeter theory has been pointed out several times in the literature [270, 134, 193, 271,
272]. The field extensions they produce, though, are rather different than the cyclotomic
extensions we encounter so far. The most important difference is that they are not of
the Galois-type because they fail to be normal. Consider a Salem number θ and its field

228



extension Q(θ). Because Q(θ) is purely real, it cannot contain all the complex roots of the
minimal polynomial for θ. This means that the extension Q(θ) is not normal because the
rational extension Q(θ) fails to be the splitting field for the characteristic polynomial of θ.

However, the rational field extension Q(θ) becomes normal over its maximal real sub-
field, Q(θ + θ−1). This is why the term Salem extension refers to the quadratic extension
Q(θ)/Q(θ + θ−1) and not to Q(θ) itself [273]. And indeed, this is the relevant field for us,
as we will see in Section A.3. The extension Q(θ)/Q(θ+ θ−1) is Galois; its only non-trivial
automorphism is the one that swaps the two elements of the pair, i.e. θ → θ−1, thus pre-
serving the base field and acting as an automorphism of Q(θ). For now, we note that there
exist an automorphism, let’s call it ω, that achieves the following map:

ω : θ0 = θ + θ−1 = eϑ0 + e−ϑ0 = 2 coshϑ0 7−→ θi = eiϑi + e−iϑi = 2 cosϑi. (A.7)

Since θ + θ−1 > 2 and the other roots sit on S1 (they are constrained −2 < θi < 2), the
automorphism ω practically maps a real number strictly larger than 2 into some number
inside (−2, 2). In other words, it turns a real θ0 into some imaginary iθi, which turns the
hyperbolic cosine cosh into a normal cosine cos. This idea will be used in Section 9.2.2.

But now the question is, where does this automorphism that exchanges the “traces”
of the pairs of roots {θ0, θ1, θ2 . . . } live in? Is it an automorphism of Gal(Q(θ)/Q(θ +
θ−1)? Well, it cannot be, because |Gal(Q(θ)/Q(θ + θ−1)| = 2 and we already discussed
its automorphism. To find where it belongs to, one must pass onto a larger field, known
as the Galois closure of Q(θ), which contains both real and imaginary roots [274]. This
is different for the cyclotomic fields, where the automorphisms that mapped the different
Coxeter planes to one another where actually living within the original rational extension
(see, for example, the case of H4 and the decomposition of 8 from the previous section).
But nevertheless, such an automorphism is guaranteed to exist, but one needs to be careful
to define in which field it lives naturally.

A.2 Minkowski Embedding: Fields as Lattices

Here, we emphasize a significant connection – due to Minkowski (§3 in [59]) – between
number fields and lattices that makes the geometry of numbers apparent.

We saw in our preliminaries section that within any number field K there exist its ring
of integers OK which has the natural algebraic structure of a free Z-module. A lattice
– as defined in Section 6 – is nothing but the integer span of some basis, again, a Z-
module. Mapping a number field to a lattice i appropriate dimensions is formalized by the
Minkowski embedding, a construction connecting number theory and geometry.

This generalizes, or perhaps elucidates, techniques already developed in [275, 276, 277, 278,

B.1 Graph-Origami Techniques

Given a Coxeter-Dynkin graph, what can you do to it to produce new graphs from it? Here,
we are interesting in processes that either fold a graph down to another graph, similarly to
how one would fold a piece of paper along some crease and identify opposite sides, or unfold
a graph into some bigger graph, similarly to how an already folded piece of paper can be
unfolded and the identified sides are now distinct. For this reason, we call the techniques
developed here graph origami.

Folding by Graph Colouring

While these foldings by graph automorphisms are generally interesting for Lie algebras,
here we are primarily concerned with foldings that lead to non-crystallographic groups,
like those shown in Fig. 6.4. These foldings are not guided by a graph automorphism, but
by a different graph property: bicolourability. Hence, to treat those, we would need to go
beyond the standard literature, and the framework developed so far can deal with these
cases in an elegant way.3

A graph is referred to as ‘bicolourable’ (or, more commonly in mathematical literature,
‘bipartite’) if its vertices can be separated into two disjoint and independent subsets – we
saw the definition in Sections 6 and 8.1. Let’s dive straight into an example to see how
the method works in these cases but also, and perhaps most importantly, how they differ
from the folding-by-automorphisms cases we dealt before.

Folding is Always a Geometric Projection

We have seen so far that folding always corresponds to a geometric projection onto an
appropriate folding subspace U . In the case of the folding-by-automorphisms picture, U
is specified entirely by the automorphism, whereas in the folding-by-colouring picture, U
is singled out by the Coxeter element of the original graph. One could say that in the
first case, the projection happens entirely along a rational direction of the crystallographic
lattice (i.e. the block-sum roots are already within U), whereas in the second case it happens
along an irrational one (one would need the projectors to introduce the relative irrational
scaling, as for A4 ↠ I52 ). But in any case, folding can always be seen as a projection: the
question is always about how to find the correct folding subspace.

As it turns out, the Coxeter element has always the answer for this. Its eigenplanes
contain all the information we need to specify U , construct the projectors and get patterns
of maximal symmetry. Familiar examples from lower dimensions include:

B4 ↠ I82 : projection of the hypercube with maximal symmetry.

A4 ↠ I52 : projection of A4’s Voronoi cell (the permutohedron) with maximal symmetry.

F4 ↠ I122 : projection of the 24-cell with maximal symmetry.

In particular, in the coloured Coxeter eigenbasis, all block-generators become immedi-
ately block-diagonal. Note that this happens only for the coloured eigenbasis and not for
any other Coxeter element: even though any two Coxeter element will share eigenvalues
(for tree-like graphs), their eigenbasis will be different. So if one uses a different Cox-
eter element than the coloured one, then one needs to also find the change of basis that
block-diagonalizes the generators separately.

The importance of the Coxeter element for folding is studied in the next subsection.

B.1.2 The Coxeter Element Criterion

The question here is the following: are all possible foldings we could think of for a given
graph admissible? In other words, given a Coxeter group G and its graph, we can always
partition its nodes in certain ways to define block reflection-generators according to the
techniques of the previous section that could give the Coxeter relations for another group
H. The question is: have we actually showed that H is a valid folding, in a sense that
there exist a folding subspace U with the properties described before?

B.1.3 Unfolding

Up to this point, we saw how to perform a folding and we developed a framework that can
handle all the interesting for quasicrystals cases of folding-by-colouring. In the language
of the Coxeter pairs, given a pair (GC , GNC) we know how to fold GC to get GNC . We can
also check whether some folding of GC is admissible. We also know that, given two known
graphs, if the eigenvalues of the Coxeter element for GNG are not all included in those of
the Coxeter element for GC , then we will not be able to perform the folding GC ↠ GNC ,
so GNC and GC do not form a Coxeter pair.

For our purposes, especially in the context of hyperbolic Coxeter groups where no Cox-
eter pairs are known (see Chapter 9), it would be interesting to know the reverse process
also, i.e. starting from a non-crystallographic graph GNC , can we unfold it into a crystallo-
graphic higher-dimensional lattice? We call this process unfolding (or embedding). One
could reasonably argue that this process is hopeless: if folding is a projection, how could
one possibly guess the lost dimensions of the projecting space from the lower-dimensional
one? As we will see, the number fields hold the memory of the higher-dimensional embed-
ding space. The idea is inspired by [279, 278] and the Minkowski embedding for number
fields (see Appendix A). If the reader has not read that Appendix, now might be a good
time to do so.

We believe this idea is best described first through a familiar example, that of H4 ↪→ E8,
as we now turn to explain.

B.2 Coxeter Pairs via Unfolding: Icosahedral Family

Finally, in this section we give the first results of a more general program about classifying
all possible Coxeter pairs and thus sCNP schemes for producing quasi-crystalline patterns
with these non-crystallographic symmetries. We begin with unfolding the icosahedrally
symmetric Euclidean GNC ’s; then, we show how to unfold several of the simplicial non-
crystallographic cases from [65] that have their entries also in the golden field Q(ϕ). In
a future work, we will deal with the rest of the non-crystallographic cases from [65] with
entries in different number fields.

Our notation closely follows that of [134]. For each spherical Coxeter graph, one can
adjoin a single extending node to obtain an affine diagram (see Fig. 6.1). Attaching one
more node to the affine cases (with a single edge), we get hyperbolic graphs: we denote them
by Ahn+2, Bhn+2, Dhn+2 and Ehn+2. Note that E10 = Eh10. The notation L353 indicates
a linear graph with three edges whose labels are 3, 5 and 3 respectively. Similarly, K53

indicates a linear graph with labels 5 and 3, but with an additional node attached to the
last node with a simple line. For hyperbolic extended graphs, if an underlying hyperbolic
graph is known, we denote the corresponding extended graph by a superscript with as
many “+” signs as the number of extending nodes.

C.1 What Can a Single Mirror Intersect?

A given vector r in Md defines a codimension-1 hyperplane through the origin, its reflection
mirror M . Depending on the nature of of the norm of r, its mirror could intersect the
following surfaces (see Fig. C.1):

• Timelike Vectors: if r is timelike, then its mirror M lies completely outside of
the lightcones C± and intersects only the de Sitter hyperboloid dSd−1 at a spacelike
surface. Such mirrors are called spacelike (since their normal is timelike). Reflections
across spacelike mirrors do not preserve the lightcones C± or the timelike hyperboloids

instance, v1 = (2, 1) and v2 = (2,−1). We can see that by taking arbitrary R-linear
combinations of them we can define a timelike vector or a null vector. However, two
timelike vectors and their scalar multiples cannot generate a spacelike direction. In this
sense, considering only spacelike roots is appropriate for describing the more fundamental
transformations.

Finally, let us comment on how mechanism 1 is included in mechanism 2: if a pair
of mirrors is already diverging, then there is at least one rank-2 principal minor that is
negative. Every larger submatrix containing this pair will also have negative determinant,
and since there are always precisely one negative eigenvalue for our hyperbolic Coxeter
groups 2, any vertex involving an this divergent pair is automatically ultra-ideal, and the
diagnosis is immediate from a single off-diagonal Schläfli entry.

C.3 Simplicial Hyperbolic Crystallographic Groups with
Ideal Vertices

In this last section of the appendix, we would like to comment on three different types of
simplices we can have according to the above vertex classification.

First of all, a simplex in (d − 1)-dimensional space like Hd−1 requires the minimum
number of bounding mirrors, which is d; in that sense, it is “simple”. In Section 8.1.2, we
mentioned that these ultra-ideal vertices for the integer self-dual lattices, which correspond
to having dashed lines in the Coxeter graph, start to appear in dimension 18, and we give
the graphs in Appendix D. These groups have more than d simple roots, thus more than
d fundamental mirrors, and thus their Coxeter polyhedron is way more complicated than
a simplex.

However, we will see crystallographic groups whose Coxeter graph has exactly d simple
roots and yet they still have ultra-ideal vertices because they contain hyperbolic subdia-
grams. By the usual definitions, since the bounding mirrors are still d, they must bound
a simplex, but this will now have infinite volume (from the point of view of Hd−1 which G
is supposed to tessellate by reflections). So how does such a simplex look like in Md?

Using the above classification of vertices and the intuition we got from our analysis,
we end up with the simplices shown in Fig. C.2. When ultra ideal vertices are present,
those must live on a spacelike point in the ambient Minkowski space Md, which means
that to close the simplex, one must look at the de Sitter hyperboloid dSd−1 for the missing
non-ordindary vertices. From the point of view of the tessellating space Hd−1, such an
unbounded simplex has infinite volume. But because all the mirrors see each other in the
ambient space and they do intersect (because all their dihedral angles are well-defined and
equal to some π/mij), they will carve out a simplex of finite volume from Md, but with
some vertices that are timelike (ordinary) and some vertices that are spacelike (ultra-ideal).

F.2.3 The Bimodal Model for the Boost Catastrophe in (1 + 1)D

We saw in Fig. 11.5 that, if we boost the integer lattice I1,1 beyond a certain threshold
ϖcrit, then the variance grows without limit. Here, we prove the equation used in that

The sampling procedure in (2+1)D is very similar to the one in (1+1)D. For each volume
V♦, we sample uniformly a rapidity ϖ in some interval [ϖmin, ϖmax] (usually taken to be
[0, 5]) and an angle φ ∈ [0, 2π]; we restrict to only positive ϖ and allow φ to run in the
entire S1, which allows us to capture the negative boosts as well.

From these parameters, we calculate the tips p♦,q♦ of ♦ = I[p,q]. A point x = (t, x, y)
is inside a diamond ♦ if and only if it is inside the future lightcone of its past tip and inside
the past lightcone of its future tip. Mathematically, we demand that (see Eq. (11.1))x ∈ Fut(p♦) ⇒ ∆tp ≥ 0 and ∆t2p ≥ s2p

x ∈ Past(q♦) ⇒ ∆tq ≥ 0 and ∆t2q ≥ s2q

where ∆tp = t−tp and ∆tq = tq−t are the temporal differences and s2p = (x−xp)2+(y−yp)2
and s2q = (x−xq)2+(y−yq)2 are the spatial ones. The number of points from some pattern
P inside a given diamond ♦ is

Here, we do not use pre-generated patches: since all structures are lattices apart from the
sprinkling, we know analytically the points and we can enumerate which ones belong to a
given ♦ once we know the tips of a boosted diamond. This allows us to test all boosts up
to our choice for ϖmax without having to care about finite-size effects and their restrictions
on ϖmax for each V♦. Finding the points in the interior of a causal diamond amounts to
solving the above inequalities over the integers in Mathematica.

F.2.9 Can We Sample in a Lorentz-Invariant Way?

We should mention that the sampling of causal diamonds performed here could be im-
proved, and one improvement would be to sample somehow with a Lorentz-invariant mea-
sure. Of course, since the Lorentz group is non-compact, such a measure is difficult to
find, which is why we decided to sample boosts uniformly in an interval. Perhaps what we
could do is to use the metric and sample tips of causal diamonds based on that (i.e. fixing
a volume and a tip and then using the metric to find the other tip). We leave all this for
future work, but, to the best of our knowledge, our setup here seems to match the setup
in [211], if not being better.

abstracts.value: We formulate fermionic particle creation in a time-dependent curved spacetime as the exact evolution of a physical Bloch vector. Each Dirac momentum mode reduces to a two-level system, and its instantaneous occupation is obtained by projecting the physical state onto the instantaneous energy basis. This construction is equivalent to the standard Bogoliubov description while retaining the complete finite-time state trajectory in a compact real geometry. It also makes the fermionic occupation bound manifest without attributing its microscopic origin to geometry alone. For a massive Dirac field in de Sitter spacetime, the dynamics reduces to a universal function of the physical momentum in Hubble units and the mass-to-Hubble ratio. We identify a mass-controlled nonadiabatic scale and a singular small-mass boundary layer that resolves the noncommuting massless and late-time limits. Independent Cartesian Bloch, angular Bloch, and Bogoliubov integrations verify the analytical results and recover the standard Gibbons–Hawking Fermi–Dirac plateau. •Exact SU(2) dynamics resolves basis-specified finite-time fermion occupation.•de Sitter modes obey an exact universal scaling in x = -k<math altimg="si1.svg" display="inline" id="d1e1205"><mi>η</mi></math> and m/H.•Nonadiabatic production peaks at physical momentum <math altimg="si2.svg" display="inline" id="d1e1215"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msqrt></mrow></math>.•Massless and late-time limits do not commute, producing a boundary layer.•Bloch and Bogoliubov integrations agree throughout finite-time evolution.

abstracts.value: In this work, we investigate the existence of traversable wormhole solutions within <math altimg="si45.svg" display="inline" id="d1e727"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> gravity by assuming higher-order curvature model <math altimg="si143.svg" display="inline" id="d1e740"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">=</mo><mi>R</mi><mo linebreak="goodbreak" linebreakstyle="after">+</mo><mi>α</mi><msup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>γ</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math>. The investigation is performed using three well-established galactic dark matter halo profiles: the Universal Rotation Curve (URC), Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) model-I, and NFW model-II. By solving the modified field equations, we establish that these dark matter distributions are capable of generating physically acceptable wormhole shape functions that satisfy the wormhole geometries (e.g. flare-out condition at the throat) for appropriate choices of the model parameters. Additionally, we investigate the associated effective energy conditions, obtained from the total (matter plus curvature-induced) stress–energy content of the modified field equations, and show that the effective null energy condition (NEC) is violated in the vicinity of the throat. This violation is a generic geometric requirement of the flare-out condition at a traversable wormhole throat and is not, by itself, a statement about dynamical stability, which is not addressed in the present work. Our findings suggest that, within the context of non-linear <math altimg="si45.svg" display="inline" id="d1e781"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo>(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></math> gravity, realistic galactic dark matter halos can act as effective sources for sustaining wormhole geometries. This establishes a potential link between dark matter phenomenology and higher-order curvature corrections in gravitational theory.

abstracts.value: We employ a single worldline effective field theory in a Schwarzschild-Tangherlini background to compute the gravitational Compton amplitude up to third post-Minkowskian order. After excising the infrared divergences associated with the Weinberg phase, we establish a direct and exact map to results in black hole perturbation theory with a natural resummation and regularization of the forward divergences of the Compton amplitude. We also outline possible applications of this useful computational bridge for Compton amplitudes that include spin and tidal effects.

titles.title: From the Gravitational Compton Amplitude to Black Hole Perturbation Theory
